item.content:encoded: Humans have prized marble for its colours, patterns, texture and heft for thousands of years. In this video, Mary McGillivray, a digital creator and PhD student at the University of Melbourne, explores how, for as long as we’ve prized it, we’ve been inventing ways to fake it. McGillivray traverses Europe to investigate how, from ancient Rome to modern home-improvement stores, we’ve developed techniques to cast, plaster and paint imitations of the metamorphic rock. And, as McGillivray argues, this process has been about more than finding a cheap alternative to a luxury material. Rather, the millennia-long history of our fascination with marble, and of our attempts to recreate it, has much to say about how humanity is inspired by, and competes with, the natural world.

item.title: Chasing la dolce vita
item.dc:creator: Ben Faccini
item.description:
Homecomings, fantasies, food and ghosts – how the myth of eternal return keeps the Italian diaspora in a state of longing

- by Ben Faccini

Read on Aeon
item.content:encoded:
When he was a child growing up in Emilia-Romagna, my great-grandfather Marco once found an eagle fledgling that had fallen from its nest. He kept it warm in the folds of his shirt and ran home, only to discover as he undressed that the bird had eaten strips of his flesh, its beak tinged red with blood. The rescued eagle thrived in my great-grandfather’s care, its wingspan soon a remarkable length. And all the while, Marco himself grew immensely tall. Then, one day, without warning, the eagle flew away.

The moment my father told me this story when I was a boy, it lodged itself deep in my imagination. I pictured young Marco as a giant striding through the forests of north-central Italy, calling to the bird of prey, waiting in vain for it to land on his outstretched hand. Marco merged with the heroes of my illustrated classical civilisation books, earning his place between the busts of Roman emperors and the chapters on Greek mythology.

What I never realised was that this family legend held clues to who I am and to my relationship to Italy.

Lina Stores deli in Soho, London, has been a pillar of Italian life in England for decades. It’s where we’d sometimes meet our paternal grandparents when visiting London from our home in France. My brothers and I would line up in front of the refrigerated counter and ask for our favourite ravioli, doing our utmost to avoid any slip-ups in Italian that would make the staff wince: ‘ricotta e spinaci’, ‘zucca’, ‘funghi porcini’. Back at our grandparents’ flat, Nonna served the ravioli on an elaborately laid table, and my grandfather appeared with freshly grated Parmigiano. He’d sprinkle the cheese evenly over our pasta; never too much, nor too little. How he did this, and with such speed, we didn’t know. If we had spaghetti, Nonna would wrap her right hand around ours and twirl the fork with us so we held just the right amount, the bespattered tablecloth damning proof of our slapdash habits at home.

My grandparents trusted that these rituals of the table (they saw them as basic codes of Italianness, connecting displaced Italians everywhere) would allow us to paper over the differences in our ethnically blended and peripatetic family. In this way, we’d be able to claim Italian identity for ourselves, despite its competition in our lives with Englishness and Frenchness. It would anchor us, or so they believed, and prevent us being bullied and singled out.

Revving their Vespas and wearing clothes I’d have avoided, they couldn’t make head nor tail of me

Every summer, on car journeys to Italy we’d listen and re-listen to Italian songs and fairytales to drum the language into us. Once we’d crossed the Alps, any stopover became an opportunity for my father to immerse us in further knowledge. He kept a torch in his pocket, and in the stillness of churches he’d let the beam scurry over frescoes until it hovered, halo-like, above a painted face or a feature in the background. ‘Such bellezza,’ he’d whisper, ‘look at the beauty of that.’ In explaining Masaccio’s brushstrokes, or playing Verdi and Puccini arias at car-shaking volume, we sensed my father was offering us, his sons, yardsticks by which to measure life. He needed us to see ourselves as the inheritors of a civilisation unlike any other. Italianness was his gift to us.

In my teens, I spent a month in Florence looking after the child of a couple of scientists, colleagues of my father. My role was to speak to the boy in English; his parents’ job was to improve my Italian. The moment I was alone with the seven-year-old, he locked himself in his room and refused to come out. As a consolation, one evening, I was entrusted to a 16-year-old nephew who took me to join his friends in a packed central piazza. Within minutes, the assembled youngsters were trying to identify my hybrid accent, crowding round with questions, trying out their English: ‘Are you French or British?’ ‘Which football team do you support?’ ‘Have you got a girlfriend?’ Revving their Vespas, blasting music I didn’t recognise, and wearing clothes I’d have avoided, they couldn’t make head nor tail of me. I escaped into Florence, only vaguely aware of where I was going. Leaning against a wall on the banks of the Arno, the Ponte Vecchio in the distance, I tried to convince myself that the surrounding ‘bellezza’ vaunted by my father was mine, that I fitted into the circus of Italian life I’d seen in Fellini films, but I felt I was a baffling anomaly, an impostor. The chameleon skills I’d always employed to fudge my way through existence had let me down. My hosts were in a state of panic on my return. Where had I been? I wasn’t going to be allowed out again. I’d failed as a childminder. And as an Italian.

A cousin recently emailed me photographs of my great-grandfather Marco, the first to set the family’s migrations in motion. I was surprised to see that he was as tall as the family legend of the eagle would have it, towering over others, but also that he was standing in front of what was the Italian Hospital in Queen Square, Bloomsbury, the place he’d apparently helped to run. This was the very spot in London I’d sat on many occasions when, as a student at King’s College, I’d search for quiet garden squares in which to read and revise for exams. I’d always believed I was drawn to the Italian Hospital because of its name. But I remember how, more than once, I’d had to get up and leave, overwhelmed by an inexplicable sadness. In another photograph, Marco was posing with my great-grandmother Delfina, also from Emilia-Romagna, on a patch of grass in Hyde Park. I recognised it immediately as the hidden slope leading down to the Serpentine lake where I often go.

After an online census revealed my great-grandparents’ old address on Highbury Fields, the sorrow I experienced outside the Italian Hospital returns. But this time its source is evident: we used to take our children to the playground by that house, parking right by my great-grandparents’ front door, our shouts and chatting rebounding off the windows. All these coincidences can doubtless be rationally explained, yet they leave me feeling that I live in the wake of tumultuous decisions made long before I was born, that I’m in a web of unseen connections, in friction with the mysteries of an uprooted Italian past.

Dressed in British suits, all the more impeccable to hide his suffering, Marco would declare that he was finally home

In 1940, when Mussolini declared war on Britain and France, all the ‘enemy aliens’ living in Britain had to be imprisoned, or as Winston Churchill put it: ‘Collar the lot!’ Marco, along with thousands of other Italians, and Germans, was rounded up and interned on the Isle of Man. As Rachel Pistol writes in ‘Enemy Aliens’ (2024), many Italian shops and businesses across the country were broken into and smashed by mobs. Marco was lucky not to be placed on the SS Arandora Star, a prisoner-of-war ship heading to Canada. More than 800 of these internees, including 442 Italians, died when the boat was torpedoed off the coast of Ireland. Just under a quarter were from different corners of Emilia-Romagna – some of them friends of Marco. The Italian Hospital scraped through the war and Marco returned to assist them. Researching this essay, I discovered that the building was broken into in 1947 and my great-grandmother, who was with her husband that day, died while confronting the intruders.

On a visit to Emilia-Romagna some years ago, I met old people who recalled widowed Marco’s long stays every summer. Dressed in British suits, all the more impeccable to hide his suffering, he would declare that he was finally home. Then he would leave for London again, returning the summer following, then again setting off, over and over. Just like us, his descendants.

Between the unification of Italy, in 1861, and 1985, around 29 million Italians left the peninsula. Political instability, high birth rates, natural disasters, unprofitable sharecropping (especially in the South), deprivation and overpopulation were major drivers for this exodus. And the more people left en masse, the more they encouraged others to join them. Today, about 80 million people outside Italy claim full or partial Italian ancestry. This diaspora has generated Little Italys across the world: in New York’s Manhattan, in La Boca, Buenos Aires, and in Clerkenwell, London. Once oases of solidarity, home-away-from-home citadels, where you could find anything – from the Italy football kit to keyrings with Leonardo da Vinci’s Vitruvian Man – they now mostly feel like places of historic, even faded, hyper-Italianness. By 1920, São Paulo alone was home to 70 per cent of the Italians who emigrated to Brazil; as many as 60 per cent of Argentinians have a link to Italy, and Italian is still one of the main mother tongues spoken in Toronto, Canada. In Australia, 4.4 per cent of the population is of Italian heritage. In America, around 17 million people identify as Italian.

Descendants of Italian migrants generally express an intense pride in their heritage, and many continue to live by its sociocultural tenets in spite of decades, or more, of absence. It is as if time away from Italy, and geographical distance, only amplify a yearning for it. Stanley Tucci, to cite but one well-known example (the same could probably be said of Lady Gaga or Francis Ford Coppola) begins his TV food series Searching for Italy (2021-22) by stating in his broad American accent: ‘I’m Italian on both sides.’

Every summer, as per my own family’s tradition, members of this diaspora return to Italy. They enjoy the peninsula in the heat-filled months: sea, mountains, food, art and music, and its dolce vita. Where Italians living in Italy might imbue their identity with more intrinsically regional elements, the diaspora, in its dissemination around the globe, carries with it a more all-encompassing interpretation of the country. Their version of Italy, like the one I grew up with, is capable of brushing over fractures and complications, and the darker sides of the nation, articulated as it is by ideals that extoll the peninsula as a connected whole.

For bona-fide Italians, a tomato sauce is never just a sauce, but a form of alchemy

By upholding and publicising the symbols of Italy – fashion, art, food, football – the diaspora has helped turn them into a recognisable shorthand for the country abroad. Visiting London’s Italian restaurants with my family, I’m struck by how many still have straw-clad Chianti bottles on the tables, and a packet of grissini tucked next to the plates, not to mention waiters who make a show of noisily grinding pepper onto our food. The performative nature of this overseas Italianness, its theatricality, is reinforced by walls decorated with photos of the owners posing with Italian American celebrities like Al Pacino, Robert De Niro or Sylvester Stallone. It is as if we’ve all been given roles, customers and waiters alike, in a Pirandello play that challenges distinctions between illusion and reality.

My kids love YouTube and TikTok videos in which a nonna or nonno, from a well-ordered kitchen in Italy, reveals how to make the creamiest cacio e pepe or the tastiest tomato sauce. These elderly cooks appear to embody an authentic art to being Italian that cuts through the mimicry and stagecraft. The children laugh loudest when these elderly home chefs from Italy screw up their faces in disgust when asked to taste American shop-bought pizza or frozen lasagne. ‘Do you know what merda means in English?’ one asks.

For bona-fide Italians, a tomato sauce is never just a sauce, but a form of alchemy. In an ideal world, it is seasoned with herbs once grown by the Romans, made with San Marzano tomatoes nourished by volcanic soil, and olive oil from Puglia’s ancient groves. This level of culinary precision largely explains why Italians are baffled, outraged even, by foreigners committing offences with their cuisine – snapping dry spaghetti in two before cooking it, grating parmesan onto seafood risotto, or mixing garlic and onion as a base for the same sauce. It might seem precious to outsiders, but a belief in excellence and the purity of traditions underpins Italianness. Indeed, something akin to the formula for tomato sauce can be applied to all areas of Italian production, from coffee machines and scooters to architecture. For my father and grandparents, Italian ingenuity stemmed from the peninsula’s endemic flair. A Lamborghini or a Gio Ponti chair was simply the latest layer of sediment in an accretion of refinement that had already given rise to Brunelleschi’s Dome and Scarlatti’s sonatas.

Despite endorsing the country as the paragon of human advancement, my father routinely turned down job offers at Italian universities and research centres, choosing instead to work in France. The resulting tension, played out in frequently announced but endlessly postponed homecomings, threw us into ever more convoluted cycles of l’eterno ritorno that had already tormented my family for two generations with their toing and froing between the peninsula and Britain. Now, with a family of my own, and living and working in London, I’m aware of how I’m resuscitating the dilemmas my parents and grandparents faced.

Increasingly, I’m hankering after Italy, wanting to pass on its rituals. I’ve made sure my children have Italian first names and a basic knowledge of Italy’s geography and history, and they seem to accept this as a given. I’ve fed them stories about eagles and ancestors, accounts of my childhood holidays in Emilia-Romagna and Tuscany, snippets of my time studying in Padua and Florence. I refer back to weddings and family gatherings we’ve all been to, seeding these memories in them, tincturing them with the aura of official history. I tell them about films they should watch one day, by Antonioni and Visconti, of the writings of Boccaccio and Dante. This visceral attachment to Italy is something I feel compelled to pass on. All the while, in parallel, I know I must value the family environment my wife and I have built in England – which is their home. It is an acknowledgement, too, of the sacrifices my ancestors made.

At times, the trap snaps shut. I sense I’m merely living out the choices of the dead, unable to escape their restlessness. Visits to Italy only temporarily assuage the feelings of unsettledness, while leaving again stirs it up. I’m losing something I’ve never owned, just as I’ve been defined by a homeland I don’t inhabit, a past I cannot alter.

Italian Americans were at times deemed ethnically ambiguous, their whiteness questioned

Perhaps, like my diasporic peers who return every summer, I find it easier to fall back on wistful memories and fantasy. I revert all too conveniently, obsessively, to the house we stayed in every year during my youth. As if in a vision, I hold on to the hoopoes in the Tuscan grassland, their heads bobbing up and down in search of insects; my parents arriving with fresh focaccia from the village; the lizards darting across the stone walls; the steady strumming of the cicadas, and the sun tensing the vineyard wires until they buzzed and sang. Warm, moonlit evenings, too, with long tables under giant oaks, friends of our parents talking and singing Italian songs late into the night, knowing no one would tell us to go to bed. I want my children to experience all this, yet I know that I can’t recreate it.

I’ve hunted for echoes of these idyllic days in Italian literature and art, and added them to the building blocks of my emigrant longing. Reading Italo Calvino’s novel The Baron in the Trees (1957), I picture the specific branches and trunks I climbed in childhood. I smell and feel the remembered coolness of stone floors and shaded high-ceilinged rooms when immersed in Lampedusa’s novel The Leopard (1958). An Andrea Mantegna painting, like The Agony in the Garden (1455-56), sends me right back to horizons dotted with hilltop villages and fortified towers of crumbling stone. I’m conscious of the pull of Italy whenever I watch its films – and the irrational reverence this triggers. Recently, I found Alice Rohrwacher’s film La chimera (2023) almost too poignant to watch as it teemed with the details of Italian life.

I know that, for every idealised image of the country, there’s a darker insinuation that Italians have had to face abroad. Late 19th-century and early 20th-century migrants from the peninsula frequently encountered discrimination – accompanied by a range of slurs, from ‘wop’ and ‘eyetie’ in Britain and the US, to ‘rital’ in France. Italian Americans were at times deemed ethnically ambiguous, their whiteness questioned, particularly when they were from the south of the peninsula. Hate-mongers, such as the Ku Klux Klan, alleged that the dregs of Italy were being sent abroad to cleanse the peninsula of its undesirables. In Protestant and English-speaking countries, Italian immigrants became easy targets because of their Catholicism, or their associations with anarchism and organised crime.

Direct conflict regularly flared up. In 1891, in New Orleans in the US, 11 Italians were acquitted of the murder of the local police chief only to be seized by a mob of thousands and lynched. In France in 1893, locals turned on Italian immigrant workers in Aigues-Mortes, reportedly killing eight men, though the number is thought to be far higher. And in 1934, in Kalgoorlie, Australia, anti-Italian killings took place against a similar backdrop of resentment against foreigners allegedly taking jobs.

Even assimilated Italians had their loyalty to their newly adopted lands questioned. It wasn’t just more recently arrived Italians like my great-grandfather who were interned as ‘enemy aliens’ during the Second World War. Some of the 4,000 men who were rounded up had spent most of their lives in Britain. This suspicion was mirrored, to a lesser degree, in Australia and the US – and this while half a million Italian Americans served in the US army during the Second World War, and 7,000 Anglo-Italians served in the British army.

In today’s world of hardening borders and changing alliances, challenges lie ahead for diaspora Italians within Italy itself. Rules for claiming Italian citizenship through ancestry or ius sanguinis (‘right of blood’) have been tightened for descendants of emigrants. This route to citizenship is now granted only to people who have a parent or a grandparent with exclusive Italian nationality, or a parent who was a citizen for two years before their birth. A 160-year history of citizenship by descent has been undermined. The question, officially at least, of who is Italian or not will be thrown into further disarray. I know from experience how hard it will be to extricate Italy from the bodies, imaginations and feelings of these figli d’italiani, these sons and daughters dispersed and far away – people who often feel they have earned the right to call themselves Italian, or at least proudly Italo-something, not least because of the stigma and rejection they or their ancestors once encountered.

At the heart of this circling around identity lies a thorny and painful question. Why do so many Italians continue to leave, and stay away? Between 2023 and 2024, 270,000 Italians emigrated, a figure considerably higher than in the previous two years. And behind the statistics lurks another grave concern: Italy’s population has been declining and is set to lose about 7 million people of working age by 2050. In 2025, there were only 355,000 births – the lowest number since the unification of Italy. In this context, the question of impossible returns is all the more troubling.

I’d like to think that there exists a worldwide collective remembrance of all things Italian, even from the days before the Risorgimento, or the movement for unification. I want to believe the countless stories of regions, cities and villages, of injustices and glories, are being kept safe by millions of descendants of emigrants who have become fervent storytellers. They are the unsung chroniclers of the peninsula, the guardians of a rich repository of traditions and customs, precisely because they have had to work harder to preserve this heritage than natal Italians. In families everywhere, from Argentina, Brazil, Canada, the US, Uruguay and Australia to France and the UK, traces of Italy remain in photographs, books and art, in buildings and the rituals of food. It is one of the paradoxes of diasporas that it is those who leave who want their country of origin to be fixed in time and preserved a certain way.

My children and I have now visited most of the spots across London where my family lived and worked. Walking further from the former Italian Hospital in Queen Square, Bloomsbury, it doesn’t take us long to reach Clerkenwell’s once-vibrant Little Italy. Though many of the delis and ice-cream parlours have been changed by new waves of immigration and redevelopment, the plaque to Giuseppe Mazzini, a champion of Italian unification, on Laystall Street, reminds passersby of the area’s historic importance to Italianness. Mass is still celebrated in Italian at St Peter’s Church, and near the back of the church is a monument to the dead of the SS Arandora Star. We sit and read the list of surnames as they mingle with the priest’s prayers to form one long lament. I picture the churches of Emilia-Romagna, and the cemeteries where my ancestors are buried, and I see the roads that lead from there to London and back, worn down by constant travelling in both directions, a straddling between nations, where ghosts are as substantial as the living.

My brothers have now exited the cycle of deferred returns by establishing families with Italian women who grew up in Italy itself. One of them has moved to Italy. In his family, Italian is, once again, the language spoken. We’ve all had to play catch-up with Italianness, but I have focused too much on the uncertainty this elicits in me. Instead, I should turn to the strength of the diasporic experience. There is power in duality, in multiplicity, and restlessness. And reassurance, too, in knowing that in London, my home, the invisible figure of my great-grandfather walks ahead of me, an eagle from Emilia-Romagna circling the sky above us.

item.title: Once upon a screen: explosive paradox
item.dc:creator: Aeon Video
item.description:
Decades after seeing ‘Platoon’, Kevin recalls how the film stirred generational trauma in his family and racism at school

- by Aeon Video

Watch on Aeon
item.content:encoded:
‘What do you think this movie is about?’

In this video essay, the US filmmaker Kevin B Lee recalls the shock of seeing, as a young film buff, the raw, violent and widely acclaimed Vietnam War film Platoon (1986) with his family in a San Francisco cinema. Recording outside the building that once housed that cinema, he details his harrowing time in the theatre and the film’s reverberations in his life beyond the theatre’s walls, including how it stirred generational trauma in his family and racism at school. With his deceptively simple approach, Lee inverts and subverts Oliver Stone’s epic, crafting, on a shoestring budget, a profound and intensely personal meditation on memory. Lee’s video essay was published as part of ‘Once Upon a Screen’, a series of video essays about film viewing and childhood trauma, commissioned and curated by Ariel Avissar and Evelyn Kreutzer, for The Cine-Files journal of cinema studies, Issue 15.

item.title: The bombarding of childhood
item.dc:creator: Natalia Kucirkova
item.description:
It’s not just screen time: the problem with children’s media is that it has become relentlessly hectic, loud and bright

- by Natalia Kucirkova

Read on Aeon
item.content:encoded:
Listen to this essay

19 minute listen

I am at the airport gate waiting to depart, watching passengers hurry past with rolling suitcases and paper cups of coffee. A small boy sits very still beside his mother. He holds an iPad close to his chest, almost in a cramp, clutching the screen as if it might otherwise run away. I hear loud clapping hands and squeaking children’s voices. I lean over and see a cartoon character in green snatch a toy from another character in pink. The pink character begins to cry, tears splashing from enormous eyes like sprinkles. The green character shouts sorry. Instantly, the tears stop and a wide smile replaces the tears before I have blinked. And, before I have even worked out whether the characters are speaking English or Arabic (as the mother does to the boy), the scene has changed and the two characters are rowing a boat with a random song in the background. The boy’s eyes dart on the screen from right to left, centre, down. His body is still but his attention is being hurried from cue to cue.

This is the problem I have come to think of as the pace of children’s media.

Children’s media are usually judged by their content and quantity: how many minutes watched and whether it was educational, age-appropriate, diverse, prosocial, commercial or safe. These questions matter and, with my colleagues, I have studied them through experiments and contributed to guidelines, regulations, or toolkits for designers. But we have been missing a bigger design feature that may be just as consequential: the time a medium gives a child to make meaning. A programme or app can contain good lessons and still move too quickly for those lessons to settle. For instance, in the US animated educational series Ask the StoryBots (2016-20), the subject matter may be genuinely rich – why the sky is blue, how eyes work, or where planets come from – but the explanation unfolds through rapid jokes, songs, visual shifts and sudden changes in style. Before a child has time to sit with one image or idea, the scene has moved on to the next, with a burst of information.

Different media have different temporal demands: a digital picture book, a game, a television episode and an app each ask a child to attend differently. But, across media, the important question is whether the pace suits the experience that the narrative claims to support. Does it give children time to follow a story, grasp a concept, identify with a character, regulate emotion or share attention with another person? Or does it continually hurry them toward the next cue, the next reward, the next burst of stimulation?

When media move too quickly, the layers of experience collapse into one another. A child may laugh at someone slipping on a banana peel but imitate only the visible silliness, missing the anticipation and reversal that make the joke work. A character may comfort a friend, but if the scene moves on too quickly, the child has little time to recognise the repair, or imagine doing the same in the kindergarten room. To develop empathy in the early years, a child must notice that another person feels something different. That small act of crossing over takes time.

In this sense, pace is not a minor stylistic feature of children’s media. It is one of the ways media imagine the child. Is the child a consumer to be retained, a nervous system to be stimulated, a vessel to be filled with educational content – or a person whose attention is still forming, and who therefore needs time to arrive?

People who worry about children and screens tend to worry about violent content, advertising, or whether a phonics app calling itself ‘educational’ truly supports phonics. These are reasonable worries and I share them. But spend five minutes watching what many young children watch, and you will see how fast, loud and bright everything on the screen has become. It does not matter whether the child is watching on a smartphone in the car or on a television at home. The screen has inherited the adult logic of media design.

That logic is, for the most part, the logic of the attention economy. It overwhelms and overshouts, making it easier for the screen to steer the viewer. The attention economy has introduced a host of small design features for shortening time. The Like button is faster than writing an appreciative comment. A progress bar tells us how many minutes remain in an article before we have decided whether to read to the end. Increasingly, AI appears beside long documents with an offer that sounds helpful but carries a philosophy: this text is long; would you like a quick summary?

The child is swept along by urgency rather than invited to dwell on responsibility or care for the other

There are, of course, features that work in the opposite direction. The delayed message and the pop-up that asks: ‘Are you sure you want to delete this?’ are two examples. Such features interrupt automatic action and return a fragment of judgment to the user. A nature documentary with linearity and the interpretive presence of an adult voice is a great model for children’s media; for example, in the TV show Prehistoric Planet (2022-25), David Attenborough’s voiceover and the camera’s zoom-ins encourage children to look closely and wonder about unfamiliar life. But these are exceptions within a larger system in which speed is treated as the default.

When learning is crowded with content that keeps jumping ahead – a crisis appears, a mission begins, a spaceship launches, a door opens – the child’s attention is restarted as each problem is introduced and immediately solved. Such media may gesture at teamwork or perseverance, but the speed of the format leaves little time for those lessons to sink in. In the animated TV series Paw Patrol (2013-), for instance, a rescue is clear and reassuring: someone is in trouble, pups assemble, each uses a skill, and order is restored. Yet the movement from problem to rescue to resolution is often so efficient that the child is swept along by urgency rather than invited to dwell on responsibility or care for the other. Similarly, in the app-based game Hot Wheels Unlimited, building tracks and racing cars may suggest creativity and problem-solving, but the dominant rhythm is acceleration: boost, race, crash, win, unlock, repeat.

Research has told us many useful things about children’s media. We know that some educational television (like Sesame Street) can support learning. We know that some apps are better designed than others. We know that interactive features in digital books can help when they serve the story, and distract when they do not. We know that characters and narratives shape children’s ideas about identity, gender and social life. Pace cuts across all of these questions as the condition under which content becomes experience.

Screen time can run fast or slow. This is partly why merely clocking ‘screen time’ is too crude a measure. Two children may each watch 20 minutes of media and have entirely different encounters with time. In one case, the child is moved through a coherent story with pauses, repetitions and recognisable emotional beats. In another, she is pulled through 10 clips, 30 characters, flashing colours, sudden songs and rewards that arrive before thought has had time to form. The clock records the same duration but the child does not live the same time.

And parents are rightly worried: a four-year-old does not come to media with adult reserves of self-regulation. She is still learning how to stay with a feeling, how to wait for a story to unfold, how to connect one event to another, how to notice that a character’s sadness matters before the joke wipes it away. If a programme moves too quickly, it may encourage a child to expect information to arrive in rapid, constantly shifting bursts, making slower, more sustained forms of attention harder to tolerate. Stopping this vicious cycle starts by asking what exactly makes children’s media fast or slow.

A child can look intensely engaged while being given very little time to think

Don’t get me wrong, I am not saying that slow is always good or better than fast media. Some lively children’s media can be excellent; some slow media can be dull, inert or badly made. The point is that good children’s media give a child time to complete an act of attention. Bad media keep interrupting that act before it can become a memory or play.

When my research group compared children’s shows, apps and digital stories, we saw that pace can become a set of design choices. A story can move in a way that helps a child anticipate what comes next, or it can jump so quickly between scenes that cause and effect become blurred. A screen can guide the eye toward one important object, or fill the frame with competing movement.

This is why the familiar adult language of ‘engagement’ is so poor for children. A child can look intensely engaged while being given very little time to think. In the Children’s Slow Media Project, we have therefore tried to make these differences visible. We evaluate children’s media by looking at how these media organise time. We ask whether the narrative is coherent enough to follow; whether the sensory field overwhelms meaning-making at specific age junctures; whether the design builds in stopping points, where the story can be digested before it goes on. Does a piece of media allow learning to develop through meaningful repetition? And does a story or piece create openings for a child and adult, or two children, to notice something together?

When in March 2026 the UK Department for Education advised parents of children aged under five to choose ‘slow-paced, age-appropriate’ content, without saying what slow-paced actually is, our group sought to make the term concrete.

What makes a show slow or fast for a given child? It depends. Children differ by age, temperament, language, sensory sensitivity and circumstance; thus, without testing their responses, it is impossible to provide a firm recommendation: a show that suits one four-year-old may overwhelm another. We therefore give ratings only to provide a map for adult judgment. The ratings are illustrations, inviting parents to check whether their child is being given enough time to complete an act of attention.

The shows scoring highest on the slow rubric are those that leave room around the characters’ actions and allow the child to recognise the actions. Often there is a face, a puppet, a song, a greeting, a familiar body on screen that treats attention as a relationship. Indeed, the power of programmes such as the US show Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood (1968-2001), the Norwegian series Fantorangen (2007-), and the British shows In the Night Garden… (2007-09) and Teletubbies (1997-2001) lies in their ability to build a rapport with the child and then repeat, almost as in a ritual. Here, small acts and greetings or songs provide a familiar frame, almost like a safety net, within which new concepts can be introduced. In the Australian animated series Bluey (2018-24), play often begins in an ordinary family situation and develops into imaginative games that involve parents, siblings and friends; the pace can be lively, but it tends to return the child to pretend play, negotiation and emotional understanding. In the animated TV series The Adventures of Paddington (2019-25) – a British-French co-production – gentle mishaps are usually held inside a world of curiosity, politeness, family and repair, so comedy becomes a route into perseverance or social understanding. Such programmes are slow because they leave openings through which the story can travel back into meaning and play.

The child’s attention is kept in motion by a manipulative rhythm that continuously restarts attention with the next tune, next bright image, next comic beat

Conversations between characters are another way in which higher-ranked shows convey new concepts with appropriate pace. When introduced with context, a new word or idea might not be immediately clear, but the child can notice and infer. Over time, the child arrives at understanding, and this slow, even arduous process helps the concept stick. For example, in one episode of Daniel Tiger’s Neighbourhood (2012-) – based on Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood – Daniel is nervous about trying the swing. The scene allows that feeling to be acknowledged, sung through, and gradually transformed into confidence, with support from Daniel’s friend Jodi and her grandmother. Similarly, in the Sesame Street-based game app Elmo Loves ABCs, a letter is traced, sounded, repeated, connected to words, and encountered through touch and play.

The lowest-scoring media are those in which the child’s attention is kept in motion by a manipulative rhythm that continuously restarts attention with the next tune, next bright image, next comic beat, next loop of familiarity or personalised nudge. Instead of allowing the child to settle into the story, such children’s shows repeatedly pull attention back; the same is true of many preschool game apps built around loops of reward and progression.

Evaluating children’s popular media taught me that pace is a revealing measure of quality but also a proxy for a deeper question about the child’s agency, their own sense of self.

The real distinction is whether a medium leaves room for the child’s own attention or continually redirects it. When every pause is filled, every uncertainty immediately resolved and every wandering thought pulled back by a brighter cue, waiting and reflection can begin to feel intolerable. The child learns to reach for the next stimulus before the previous one has had time to settle. To give space for a child’s attention to drift inward, to reflect, is therefore to leave room for the child’s inner life. Slow media changes the relation between screen and child by saying: you may arrive at your own pace.

Some critics may dismiss slow media as nostalgia: a longing for the children’s television of the previous generation, or a privilege available only to parents with time and large bookshelves and big houses with quiet rooms. But that is a notion we should refuse. The attention economy has trained us to treat a child’s pause as a problem, a wandering gaze as lost engagement, and an unfilled moment as wasted time. The opposite is true – slow time gives children the space to perceive, process, respond and make meaning – and it can be designed for in children’s media.

Like energy drinks, fast media promise more capacity than the child actually has: more attention is supposed to lead to better performance. Fast media feel like an extension of the child’s energy, but the bargain is unsustainable and unhealthy. What looks like support can become dependency, and what promises engagement and learning is actually compulsion.

Children need media that do not merely occupy them, instruct them or keep them quiet. They benefit and grow from stories and shows that preserve children’s capacity for inwardness and their relation to others. In fast media, the child’s attention is continually propped up by the next stimulus. Slow media insist on the opposite. In the end, the aim is not to withdraw children from the digital world, but to make that world more worthy of them.

item.title: Penchants of the polymaths
item.dc:creator: Mariam Sabri
item.description:
The fathers of Islamic science hold lessons for students: breadth over specialisation, and never let constraints get in the way

- by Mariam Sabri

Read on Aeon
item.content:encoded:
Listen to this essay

23 minute listen

This semester, my students are learning about four polymaths who shaped Islamic science: al-Biruni, Alhazen, Avicenna and al-Khwarizmi. Their circumstances could hardly have been more different: one wrote his way out of scarcity; one was held under house arrest for a decade; one distilled an era’s medical knowledge into a text that ruled European universities for 500 years; and the last worked at the largest research institution of his age. But each shared the same underlying instinct: to move freely between mathematics, medicine, astronomy, philosophy and poetry, testing one discipline’s assumptions against another’s. My classroom is in Pakistan, where students arrive eager to talk about disruption and employability, but rarely about breadth. I want them to see, through these four lives, that this kind of expansiveness isn’t a luxury for stable times; it has produced some of the most enduring breakthroughs in the history of science.

After 15 years working in liberal arts education, I believe a reintegration of disciplines in a Hellenistic style can lead the way. I’m not making a superficial case for ‘interdisciplinarity’. Instead, I’m arguing for something more specific: the recovery of the penchants of polymathy that once thrived in the Muslim world. Rather than fetishising disruptive innovation through compulsory courses on entrepreneurship and applied methods, we should offer an entirely different model of how to learn and what learning is for – especially since my students already enter university with a narrowly vocational mindset.

The word polymathy itself captures the bricolage of many (poly) worlds of knowledge (mathy). Polymathy offers respite and reflection in a world fractured by war, climate catastrophe and injustice. It is sourced from indigenous idioms of the Muslim world rather than an imposition by the Global North. Today, polymathy brings different kinds of thinking to bear on political, economic and environmental problems. At a time when students are reading less of the classic canon and worrying more about employment opportunities, the expansiveness of polymathy can offer a meaningful path forward. These are the lessons of the great Islamic polymaths.

The life of our opening actor al-Biruni has much to teach students about the human dimensions of science. Born in the Central Asian city of Khwarizm around 973, he grew up with few opportunities. But that didn’t constrain him: al-Biruni sought an education. In the classic tradition of Islamic polymathy, he studied Islamic law, grammar, theology, the sciences of astronomy and mathematics, as well as history. Throughout his life, lack was not an impediment for al-Biruni. In fact, scarcity has a way of making one appreciate whatever knowledge is at their disposal – a key lesson for any liberal artist.

This resourcefulness fuelled al-Biruni to make key contributions to his fields of expertise. Early in his career, he had limited access to scientific instruments. Undeterred, he taught himself to build them from a handful of old manuals and limited resources. Al-Biruni’s ingenuity also allowed him to take on established scientific leaders. The astronomer al-Khujandi, for instance, had built a massive sextant that he used to measure the tilt of Earth’s axis relative to its orbit (its obliquity). The number he yielded, though, struck al-Biruni as too low. Because of his experience in building his own sextants, he was able to identify the issue: al-Khujandi’s sextant sagged, distorting his results. The scarcity that had compelled al-Biruni to make his own sextants made it possible to see where others with far more resources had gone wrong. Al-Biruni’s own measurements, documented in The Determination of the Coordinates of Locations for Accurately Measuring the Distances between Places, were widely accepted by his contemporaries and later scientists.

Had al-Biruni never been compelled to travel across South and West Asia, he’d never have made this critical observation

Al-Biruni’s later life and works were shaped by Mahmud Ghazni, sultan of the Ghaznavid empire from 998 to 1030. Mahmud was a terrific military leader, reputed never to have lost a battle, who dramatically extended his unstable empire. Among the lands he conquered was al-Biruni’s native Khwarizm; al-Biruni himself was soon compelled to serve in Mahmud’s court. Under Mahmud, he travelled across Central Asia, India and the Arab lands. These years played a crucial role in shaping his intellectual contributions and the fields he chose to study.

Al-Biruni’s servitude ironically gave him the opportunity to traverse mountainous and coastal terrains, as well as to learn from the astronomical traditions of India, Persia and Arabia. His groundbreaking method for measuring Earth’s radius grew out of one of these journeys: at Nandana Fort in Punjab, he climbed a hill, measured the angle of the dip of the horizon, and calculated Earth’s radius to within a remarkable degree of accuracy (modern conversions put his figure at 3,928.77 English miles).

While most of al-Biruni’s fellow astronomers subscribed to geocentricism, he actually toyed with heliocentrism, though without formally integrating the theory into the rest of his thought (some 500 years before Copernicus). And al-Biruni’s travels to coastal areas and the Arabian deserts helped him understand the formation of canyons and composition of sand. ‘With the passing of time,’ he observed, ‘the sea becomes dry land, and dry land the sea.’ Had al-Biruni never left Central Asia and been compelled to undertake his travels across South and West Asia, he would never have made this critical observation. Al-Biruni’s life teaches students today that lack and scarcity need not be impediments; they can be resources for innovation.

Creativity can come as much from unimagined possibilities as from unforeseen limitations. The life and work of our next polymath, Alhazen, is a testament to how creativity emerges under constraints, particularly in captivity. While both poverty and captivity prompt creativity, these constraints are qualitatively different. One relates to scarcity and the other to immobility. Scarcity does not foreclose travel, while captivity – an unfortunately common experience for students working under oppressive governments today – disconnects one entirely from the outside world that offers a plethora of possibilities. These circumstances distinguished al-Biruni and Alhazen.

Alhazen (also known as Ibn al-Haytham) was a major scholar of optics, born around 965 in Basra, in modern-day Iraq, where there was a thriving intellectual climate that led to significant scientific and literary production. It was where the study of Arabic grammar was founded; where al-Jahiz explored everything from zoology to theology; where the Ikhwan al-Safa – a clandestine brotherhood of scientist-philosophers – compiled a massive encyclopaedia that wove together mathematics, music and metaphysics. It was this cosmopolitan and bookish culture that shaped Alhazen.

In his early days, he became famous for his revolutionary feats in engineering. But he outdid himself when he boldly proposed the construction of a dam on the River Nile to regulate its flow. The Fatimid caliph al-Hakim, ruling from Cairo, got wind of Alhazen’s extraordinary proposal. Known to history as the ‘Mad Caliph’, al-Hakim was a deeply eccentric and vindictive ruler, who persecuted religious minorities and once ordered that all the dogs in Cairo be killed (he was evidently annoyed by their barking). When Alhazen arrived in Egypt, he found to his dismay that the Nile could not be so easily tamed; his dam was entirely unfeasible. Reasonably fearing that his failure would upset the Mad Caliph, Alhazen himself claimed insanity. The ruse worked: he escaped execution and instead remained under house arrest until al-Hakim’s death.

Alhazen was among the first to argue that vision results from light entering the eye, not rays emitted by it

Alhazen remained under house arrest for a decade. Bound to his abode with nothing but his interests, he developed groundbreaking theories of vision in a book entitled Kitab al-Manazir (‘Book of Optics’). Given the physical limitations of his house arrest, he spent a lot of time building, tinkering and experimenting with instruments that helped him understand the behaviour of light. His vast knowledge was his sole resource during the imprisonment. As a polymath, Alhazen combined his knowledge of geometry, astronomy, optics and engineering. He developed mathematical equations to explain how light worked, studied many astronomical phenomena, especially stars, to explain theories of brightness, and used engineering principles of the camera obscura to mimic the function of the eye.

His most influential contribution remains foundational to optics. Alhazen was among the first to argue that vision results from light entering the eye, not rays emitted by it. This was his influential theory of intromission. His views put him at odds with such greats as Ptolemy, Euclid and Galen, whose emission theory of optics held that the eye projected rays onto the objects it perceived. But Alhazen countered that this couldn’t be squared with astronomy: if the eye had to send out rays before we could see anything, there’d be no way to explain how we see distant stars the instant we open our eyes.

His development of the intromission theory revealed another crucial ability: his critical thinking. His works are a testament to the fact that Muslim polymaths did not just consume, translate or replicate Greek knowledge. Rather, they critiqued and innovated. Had Alhazen not critiqued Greek science, combining his knowledge of optics, astronomy and mathematics with practical demonstrations of the camera obscura – all under conditions of captivity – his intromission theory would not have emerged.

While most believe the theories of intromission were the pinnacle of Alhazen’s intellectual achievements, but in fact his polymathy also created novel connections between optics and psychology. As the neuroscientist Charles G Gross has argued, Alhazen was ‘the first to recognise the crucial importance of eye movement for perception’, thus constituting our consciousness of the visual world. Alhazen realised that the reception of light by the eye was the first of many crucial steps in perception. His optics explained how light physically reaches the eye, but insisted that it was only the first step – turning that raw sensation into an actual conscious percept required unconscious inference, memory and comparison. It is a startlingly modern view, which wouldn’t be articulated in the West until the 19th century – and had Alhazen been narrowly wedded to a single field he would never have made this discovery.

Whether students endeavour to be scholars or entrepreneurs, they need to seek out eclectic experiences without a predetermined outcome. Alhazen’s combination of creativity and critical thinking under constraints led to the extraordinary achievements for which he is still remembered.

Perhaps the most prominent polymath from the Islamic world was Avicenna, who was intellectually active from 997 to 1037. A widely known physician and philosopher hailing from Bukhara in Central Asia, he was a child prodigy, demonstrating mastery over complex texts and concepts at a young age. While his contributions to medicine are often cited today, his contributions to the development of the scientific method were his primary achievements. Much like Alhazen, Avicenna moved fluidly from observation to experimentation, from induction to deduction, leading to his breakthroughs in medicine and philosophy as well as lesser-known contributions to psychology and geology.

Avicenna’s magnum opus, Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb (‘The Canon of Medicine’), was an attempt to compress the entire medical knowledge of his age – Greek, Persian and Indian – into a single, systematic reference. Completed around 1025, it unfolds across five books: general principles of physiology and disease; an alphabetical catalogue of some 800 medicinal substances; diseases organised by body part, from head to foot; conditions affecting the whole body, such as fevers; and a formulary of roughly 650 compound remedies. But what distinguishes the Canon is its method. Avicenna lays out the rules for testing a new drug’s effects, effectively articulating the idea of a clinical trial centuries before the term existed. Translated into Latin in the 12th century, the Canon became the standard medical textbook in European universities for more than half a millennium. Avicenna’s genius, though, lay not just in the substance of this achievement but in what we would now call science communication: he wrote lucid prose and evocative poetry.

When Avicenna was stuck on a logic problem, he headed to the mosque and prayed until his mental fog lifted

Poetry was, in fact, a key didactic device for communicating scientific knowledge in the classical world. Rhyme and meter helped make the material easy to memorise. Avicenna’s Al-Urjuzah fi al-Tibb (‘Poem on Medicine’) distilled the lessons of the Canon so that physicians could easily recall its recommendations and insights. These lines, in Haven C Krueger’s 1963 translation, evocatively capture the experience of disease:

Symptoms are obtained through physical examination of the body at certain moments. There are some visible ones such as jaundice and oedema; there are some perceptible to the ear such as gurgling of the abdomen in dropsy; the foul odour strikes at the sense of smell; for example that of purulent ulcers; there are some accessible to taste such as the acidity of the mouth; touch recognises certain ones: the firmness of cancer!

Avicenna’s contributions far outweighed medical discoveries and innovations. His contribution to the scientific method itself was groundbreaking. When he was stuck on a logic problem, he used mysticism as a method: he headed to the mosque and prayed until his mental fog lifted and he solved the puzzle. In many ways, this anticipates the role that meditation plays today in achieving mental clarity. Scientists are now finding that a change of scenery and change of pace can work wonders for researchers. Contrary to popular belief, mindfulness is not a new solution to an old problem. It is a recycled recommendation from many spiritual traditions, packaged in a palatable secularism. Seeing mindfulness through its historic uses from Buddha to Avicenna gives the practice credibility beyond its fetishisation as a disruptive approach by Silicon Valley. It is an age-old practice linked to innovation.

Whenever I assign Avicenna’s autobiography in my history of science class, my students are struck by something very simple: the intertwinement of religion and science. The two have not always been at loggerheads, as students are now ahistorically encouraged to believe. Avicenna’s own habit of praying his way through a difficult logic problem is a case in point: for him, turning to the mosque when reason stalled wasn’t a retreat from rigorous thought but an extension of it, since prayer and logical enquiry were both aimed at the same goal of grasping a difficult truth. I have lost count of the number of times students gawk at examples of scientists from history who were spiritual, not secular, without ascribing a value judgment to their belief systems. These also include relatively recent scientists such as the Nobel Laureate in Physics Abdus Salam, a Pakistani who openly identified as Muslim and saw no contradiction between his faith and his research.

Furthermore, Avicenna was not alone in using lush language to explain scientific concepts. Rhetoric was one of the main liberal arts in the Greek and Islamic traditions, and most scholars were skilled in it. That tradition persisted to 20th-century scientists such as Abdus Salam, who carried a lifelong love of poetry in Urdu, Persian, Punjabi and English, and colleagues who heard him lecture on particle physics remarked that his eloquence made the subject sound like literature. For both Avicenna and Salam, vivid language wasn’t decoration bolted on to the science after the fact; it was part of how the ideas were thought through, and how they were made to stick. Emphasising effective and evocative writing skills to students in the liberal arts classroom today is key to their success. Writing is not an isolated skill that can be replaced by AI. It is fundamental to both communication and cognition for future leaders in science and entrepreneurship. Avicenna’s life and legacy attest to both methodological eclecticism and compelling science communication in ways that are waning today due to specialisation and narrow vocational education.

Our final polymath, al-Khwarizmi, is invaluable to a liberal arts curriculum in the Muslim world and beyond. As the father of algebra and namesake of the word ‘algorithm’, his work shows that theory emerges from wrestling with practical problems and that abstraction can solve pragmatic challenges. Born in Central Asia around 780, al-Khwarizmi rose to prominence as a leader of Islamic science. He was a key scholar at the Bayt al-Hikmah (House of Wisdom) in Baghdad – then the largest institution of intellectual enquiry in the Muslim world – with a vast knowledge of mathematics, astronomy and geography that was relevant to the practical problems of governance and administration faced by the Abbasid empire.

He described his treatise on algebra, the Kitab al-Mukhtasar fi Hisab al-Jabr wa al-Muqabala (‘The Concise Book of Calculation by Restoration and Balancing’), as a practical handbook, a ‘work on algebra, confining it to the fine and important parts of its calculations, such as people constantly require in cases of inheritance, legacies, partition, law-suits, and trade, and in all their dealings with one another where surveying, the digging of canals, geometrical computation, and other objects of various sorts and kinds are concerned.’ These were all imperative applications for successful imperial administration under the Abbasids. Despite the abstract attraction of algebra, it was never meant to be a purely theoretical tradition divorced from real-world needs.

Al-Khwarizmi’s algebra grew out of practical problems – inheritance disputes, land surveys, canal digging

Al-Khwarizmi is best remembered for founding algebra, but his ambitions extended into astronomy and geography as well. In dedication to Caliph al-Ma’mun, who reigned in 813-33, he composed his own Zij al-Sindhind, astronomical tables charting the movements of the Sun, the Moon and five known planets, adapting earlier material brought to Baghdad from India. The tables included calculations for the length of shadows cast at different times of day, essential for setting prayer times and calibrating sundials. Later, in the Kitab Surat al-Ard (‘Book of the Description of the Earth’), he turned to geography, correcting and expanding Ptolemy’s centuries-old map of the world with coordinates for 2,402 locations. Across mathematics, astronomy and geography alike, the through-line in al-Khwarizmi’s work is precision: an insistence on measuring, tabulating and correcting, rather than simply inheriting received knowledge.

Theory itself is often the real barrier I see in the classroom, especially among students from geographically disadvantaged backgrounds who arrive well practised in applied knowledge but not in abstraction. The mainstream Pakistani school curriculum rewards rote learning over critical or abstract thinking, so theory can feel foreign rather than useful. Al-Khwarizmi’s life argues otherwise: his algebra grew out of thoroughly practical problems – inheritance disputes, land surveys, canal digging – but its power lay in outlasting them, becoming a method supple enough to structure problems no 9th-century administrator could have imagined. Theory, in other words, isn’t the opposite of practice; it’s what practice becomes once it’s generalised. That is the lesson worth carrying into a liberal arts classroom that too often treats abstraction as a luxury rather than a skill.

The lives of these polymaths prompt us to appreciate that constraints can lead to creativity and innovation. This is especially illustrated by the examples of al-Biruni and Alhazen, even if the nature of those constraints is different: scarcity made al-Biruni create his own instruments, while Alhazen’s captivity forced him to look inward, contemplating the connections between vision and psychology. For Avicenna and al-Khwarizmi, polymathy grew instead out of institutional patronage and courtly upheaval, which gave them both the room and the reason to move between medicine, philosophy, mathematics, astronomy and geography as they wove Greek, Persian and Indian traditions into new syntheses.

What unites the four is not the particular constraint or opportunity each encountered, but what they did with it: none let a single discipline set a boundary on their thinking. Critique was central to this refusal, too, as Alhazen’s disputation of emission theory in favour of intromission illustrates: polymaths did not simply inherit received knowledge; they interrogated it. And theory and practice were never opposed, as Avicenna’s clinical method and al-Khwarizmi’s precision-driven mathematics attest: exactitude and abstraction are as much cornerstones of a liberal arts education as breadth itself. What each of these lives shares, finally, is the cross-cultural exposure that pluralistic patronage made possible. Polymathy has never been a solitary pursuit, but one fed by contact across traditions.

That lesson matters for my students in Pakistan today, most of whom will build careers in a world reshaped by AI, climate disruption and political upheaval far more volatile than any single discipline can prepare them for. If al-Biruni, Alhazen, Avicenna and al-Khwarizmi could turn scarcity, captivity, patronage and instability into new ways of knowing, then breadth is the necessary preparation for the tremendous work ahead.

item.description:
Can we test for AI consciousness when we don’t understand our own? Getting into John Searle’s ‘Chinese room’ experiment

- by Aeon Video

Watch on Aeon
item.content:encoded: Devised by the late US philosopher John Searle in 1980, the ‘Chinese room’ thought experiment is one of the best-known challenges to the idea that programmed computers could be conscious. This animation from TED-Ed lays out Searle’s famed argument, which has drawn considerable criticism and become more contentious as AI systems have grown far more sophisticated. While exploring whether the Chinese room still computes in the AI era, the video considers the mounting complexities of ever knowing whether computers could have cognitive states – especially given how little we understand our own.

item.dc:creator: Katherine Harvey

Saffron and ostrich liver were prescribed but so were exercise, gardens, animals, socialising, and music

- by Katherine Harvey

Read on Aeon
