Early one morning in the late 12th century, Bishop Hugh of Lincoln arrived in the Hertfordshire village of Cheshunt. There, he was immediately surrounded by a crowd of people, who begged him to help one of their neighbours. And so, dismounting from his horse, he went to the man’s house, where he was confronted by the disturbing sight of a possessed man ‘lying prostrate with his head tied to a post and each of his hands to great stakes fixed in the ground.’ Despite these restraints, the man constantly writhed around, rolling his eyes, gnashing his teeth, and sticking his tongue out. To Hugh, as to the local onlookers, the diagnosis was clear: this unfortunate sailor had been possessed by a demon and could be cured only by an exorcism. Once the necessary rituals were performed, he was ‘delivered from the demon [and] … after living devoutly for some years, finally made a good and peaceful end.’

For Hugh’s biographer, Adam of Eynsham, the incident was worth recounting because it demonstrated not only that the future saint had healing powers, but that he was a brave and compassionate man (in sharp contrast to the local bishop, who had ‘galloped away as if pursued by the Furies’, rather than face a possessed man). But, to us, the story – full of fear, cruelty and superstition – sums up both everything that was wrong with medieval attitudes to mental illness, and the apparent uselessness of medieval medicine in the face of serious illness.

And yet, as is so often the case when studying the distant past, the reality was rather more complicated. Influenced by stories of demonic possession (and there are lots of them, especially in saints’ lives and miracle collections), I long assumed that our ancestors’ attitudes to, and experiences of, mental health were completely different to our own – and that they would have little sympathy with our fast-growing mental health crisis. But when I turned my attention away from religious texts, and began to research medieval ideas about healthy living, I soon came across medieval people who discussed mental health in ways that felt far more familiar to me.

The similarities were particularly apparent in medical writings, which outline a sophisticated argument that mental wellness was at the heart of a healthy lifestyle. According to the dominant humoral system of medicine, health was achieved by keeping four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile) in balance. The best way to do this was through careful management of the six non-naturals, a set of external factors that had a direct impact on the human body, and that included many of our modern preoccupations, such as diet, exercise and sleep, as well as the emotions.

This last factor featured prominently in regimens (how-to books about healthy living, which were extremely popular in late-medieval Europe), in which people were warned that, for the sake of their health, they must control their emotions. According to the 14th-century Sevillian physician Juan de Aviñón, ‘it is necessary that a man that wishes to preserve his health will not become angry, nor irritated, nor worried as much as possible, because once he does so he greatly harms his body.’ Similarly, the Bavarian physician Arnold von Bamberg warned that emotional dysregulation could disrupt an individual’s eating habits, exercise routine and ability to sleep; a person who did not pay sufficient attention to his feelings would inevitably end up needing medical treatment. And it seems that people did blame their bodily ailments on mental travails. For example, in 1395, when the Italian politician and wool merchant Niccolaio Martini was ill with a high fever, he told his friend Margherita Datini that ‘he came down with this illness after getting very upset’ about the result of a recent election.

Too much responsibility could make a person ill, with high-status men thought to be at particular risk

Certain emotions were so detrimental to health that they could cause sudden illnesses, or even death. Fear was especially dangerous: among the miracles performed by the hand of St James (which was kept at Reading Abbey from the mid-12th century) was the cure of Alice, an Essex clerk’s daughter who saw a ghost when milking sheep on Good Friday. Her terror caused the blood to freeze around her heart, and so confused her senses that she suffered a temporary fit of mania and threw herself into a fire. Anger, which warmed and dried the body, was also unhealthy; as a chronic problem, it would (in the words of one mid-15th-century German regimen) ‘consume the body swiftly, so that the man meets a short end’, while a serious temper tantrum could prove fatal. One chronicler claimed that Henry I’s final illness was caused by a dispute with his daughter, the English king being ‘provoked by these irritations to anger and bitter ill-feeling, which were said by some to have been the origin of the chill in his bowels and later the cause of his death’.

Fear and anger were usually acute emotions, quick to come and go, but medical experts also warned about the dangers of chronic emotional distress. One of my favourite medieval images compares the mind to a bent bow which, although strong, cannot survive continual strain, so that ongoing ‘disputes in the household’ could ‘shorten a person’s years’. Just as we worry about stress, medieval people recognised that too much responsibility could make a person ill, with high-status men thought to be at particular risk. In an English conduct book written around the turn of the 13th century, Daniel of Beccles claimed that a master ‘lives like a toiling ant’; his ‘pressing worries gnaw at his gut and burden his shoulders’, and his mind is ‘always focused on calamities’. The anonymous biographer of the French knight Jean II Le Meingre (c1366-1421), better-known as Boucicaut, described his packed daily schedule, but suggested that ‘those who love him indeed, those who would wish him long life and the good health which makes public duties manageable … ought rather to advise him to be a little less conscientious and to take at least some time for repose and recreation.’ If he did not do so, he would surely become ill.

Similarly, though we tend to assume that life in the medieval cloister was rather cushy, a surprising number of monks felt themselves to be under intolerable pressure. Whenever I visit Rievaulx Abbey (now a picturesque ruin in the North York Moors National Park), I spare a thought for Matthew, a 13th-century monk there, who complained to his friend William, the prior of nearby Byland, that his duties as precentor were making him ill; he felt that ‘from the bottom of my feet to the very top of my head … there is no peace in my bones’, and was also suffering from stomach pains and exhaustion. His job was, he complained, too much for one elderly man, and he was sure that it would kill him. Matthew’s fate is unknown, but some monks did suffer breakdowns that were attributed to overwork. At St Albans, Alexander de Langley first became ill when his monastic duties caused him ‘to have fits of raving and to give himself wonderful great airs’. And when his workload was reduced, he then began to study too much, which ‘in the end robbed him of his wits’.

Others were plagued by anxiety. The Tuscan merchant Francesco Datini (c1335-1410), who once wrote that ‘Fate has so willed that, from the day of my birth, I should never know a whole happy day,’ worried about almost everything, especially his business and the Black Death (which struck Italy repeatedly throughout his life, its first wave having orphaned him as a young boy). In 1395, he told his wife Margherita that ‘I dreamed last night of a house which had fallen to pieces, and all my household were inside it’; this had set him thinking about a ship of which he’d had no news for more than two months, and he felt ‘so vexed by many matters, it is a wonder I am not out of my mind.’ Inevitably, she in turn worried about him, urging him to relax for the sake of his health: on one occasion when he was ‘very worried’, she asked him ‘why dwell on it so much that you harm both body and soul?’

Datini’s anxiety seems to have been exacerbated by depressive tendencies, since Margherita also fretted that ‘What worries me most is that you seem to have been extremely melancholy, though you refuse to tell me anything…’ Like its modern counterpart, melancholia’s main characteristics were persistent low mood and a lack of interest in daily life, although sufferers might also ‘see before their eyes terrible and frightening and black shapes such as monks, black men killing them, [and] demons’. Datini’s fellow sufferers included King Duarte of Portugal (1391-1438), who wrote in moving detail about his life-long struggle with a ‘melancholic humour’, which first affected him when he served as regent during a major plague outbreak. And, once again, monks were thought to be especially vulnerable, since their many burdens (which included long periods of silence, constant church services, too much entertaining, and receiving bad news about friends) made them prone to acedia, which left them ‘so much disturbed in spirit, that they move about among their fellows as though they were half-dead.’

Fortunately for these unfortunate individuals, though medieval people did not have access to modern psychiatric medicines or therapists, the medical profession was increasingly interested in both emotional health and the mind-body connection, which informed the treatments on offer. Melancholiacs, for example, were usually thought to be suffering from an excess of black bile, which caused the brain to fill with mist, obscuring rational thought. Consequently, their doctors should address the underlying physical problem by purging the superfluous humours and increasing bodily heat, perhaps using syrups made with warming ingredients such as cinnamon and liquorice, or massage with warm oils.

More broadly, medieval people shared our interest in the ability of mind-altering substances to prevent and treat mental health problems. Saffron was widely believed to provoke joy – although one Welsh recipe collection (c1400) warned against eating too much ‘in case you die of happiness’ – and both oregano and fennel were credited with similar powers. Alternatively, a melancholiac might be advised to eat ostrich liver – a suggestion I find particularly unappealing, though I could be persuaded to test the supposed benefits of precious stones. According to Abbess Hildegard of Bingen (1098-1179), ‘If you are oppressed with sadness, [you should] look at an onyx intently, then place it in your mouth. The oppression of your mind will cease.’ She also advised that holding and looking at beryl, or placing a sapphire in one’s mouth, could calm anger.

But these remedies worked best when combined with lifestyle changes, so that patients were also told to do things that would cheer them up – much as modern doctors use social prescriptions to encourage activities that improve wellbeing. When Taddeo Alderotti treated Obizzo II d’Este, lord of Ferrara (c1247-93), who had suffered from melancholy and insomnia for more than two years, his prescription included ‘taking walks … seeing things that are beautiful and delightful to him … hearing songs and instruments that he likes … being told about and promised great yields from profitable markets’. In fact, joy was widely considered to be not just a useful cure but also an important part of a healthy lifestyle for, as one mid-15th-century German verse regimen reminded readers: ‘A sorrowful heart often brings people to the end/but the joyful mind always makes the life’s age blossom.’ While virtually every other strong emotion dried up the body, joy was good because it moistened it; other benefits included purer blood, sharper wits, higher energy levels and a healthy complexion. It could even make a person more attractive.

One ailing friar was warned to stop reading ‘horrible stories depicting martyrdoms or death’

Consequently, medical experts encouraged everyone to do things that would cheer them up and distract them from their problems – and their suggestions include many things that I (and many others around the world) still find helpful. Spending time with loved ones was an important source of pleasure for many, including Francesco Datini, whose friendship with the lawyer Lapo Mazzei (to whom Margherita once wrote ‘Pray tell Francesco some of your jests, that they may bring solace to his melancholy’) was clearly important. And, like us, medieval people often sought companionship from their pets. Cats, dogs and birds were especially popular, though Robert de Insula, bishop of Durham in 1274-83, kept monkeys ‘to ease the burden of his worries’ and Alfonso X of Castile (1221-84) had a ferret he ‘loved dearly and carried with him and cared for tenderly’.

Recent studies have shown that regular engagement with the arts can improve both our physical and mental health, and medieval people shared our belief that culture was good for them. Reading, for example, was widely considered to be a healthy activity, although it was important to choose cheerful books; one ailing friar was warned to stop reading ‘horrible stories depicting martyrdoms or death’, for the sake of his health. (As a keen reader with a particular fondness for what my sister calls ‘your sad-people books’, I feel somewhat attacked by this piece of advice.)

Many regimens also extolled the benefits of music, which was often used to cheer those facing difficult personal circumstances. In the 1390s, when a prominent Bolognese lawyer’s son was dying of ‘a destructive and horrible illness’, the city government sent him a master musician and storyteller to sustain him in his troubles, explaining that ‘constant worrying deprives individuals of their vital breath, and the best remedy for this is to listen to stories and songs as often as possible.’ Around the same time, they granted a safe conduct for a medical practitioner named Sergio of Polo, who used song to ‘calm human minds and restore weak and infirm hearts to a state of deep joy and tranquillity’.

Getting out of the house was also thought to have significant benefits for both physical and mental health, so that depressed monks were encouraged to take long walks, and wealthier monasteries often owned country houses where exhausted monks could ‘benefit from a change of air and surroundings’. Medieval people were enthusiastic about the health benefits of gardens, which provided sensory stimulation (from green grass, sweet-smelling flowers and tinkling water features), as well as opportunities for exercise and relaxation. When Francesco Datini built himself a house in his native Prato, he included a large pleasure garden ‘full of oranges, roses and violets and other lovely flowers’ – and though he latter considered that this had been ‘a great piece of folly’, since he would have made more money from a farm, he clearly derived pleasure from this indulgence. Others liked working in the garden: the humanist scholar Bartolomeo Platina (1421-81) particularly enjoyed weeding and pruning.

Gardening was good, Platina believed, because it relaxed the mind while exercising the body, and exercise was an important part of a healthy lifestyle. Though indoor activities such as weight-lifting and stair-climbing were sometimes recommended in regimens, most experts believed that the best forms of exercise were those done outdoors, such as walking. As a keen walker, I certainly agree with the London-based 15th-century medical writer John Mirfield, who explained that outdoor exercise is good not just for the body, but also for the soul and mind, ‘for then a man is exposed to wholesome air, and he rejoices in gazing far and near, and upon the sky, the sea and the green landscape; and he is therefore constrained to commend, to praise, and to magnify the Lord his God. Exercise therefore is good, since … it unites a man to his Creator.’

Mirfield’s description of outdoor exercise as something that provided physical, mental and spiritual benefits reflects the widespread belief that the health of body, mind and soul were intertwined, and that religious devotions could, by improving a person’s mood, convey the same health benefits as secular pleasures. Consequently, medical texts identified piety as a quality that would improve an individual’s health. One late-13th-century Occitan regimen included prayer as one of the activities a person must do ‘with joy’, in order to lengthen their life, while the bestselling Dietary written by the monk-poet John Lydgate (c1370-c1451) discussed moral conduct and the importance of regular devotions (a person should, for example, ‘do reverens’ to God on rising) alongside warnings to regulate one’s emotions.

And it is clear that religious belief helped many medieval people cope with difficult times. King Duarte’s experience of melancholy was shaped by his conviction that his illness was ordained by God; consequently, though he consulted physicians and made some changes to his lifestyle (including improving his work-life balance and getting more sleep), he found that devotion to God and the Virgin Mary, expressed through pious deeds such as almsgiving, confession, and taking communion, offered the greatest relief. The Florentine wool merchant Giovanni di Paolo Morelli had a similar experience when tormented by grief and guilt after the death of his eldest son – a loss on which he reflects in his memoir, one of the saddest I have ever read. He found the first anniversary of the boy’s death especially hard, as terrible dreams left him ‘desperate almost to the point of putting an end to all those adversities’. But his faith saved him.

Though taking care of one’s mental health was always important, there were times when it became crucial to one’s survival. From the first outbreak of the Black Death, many believed that a negative attitude could make a person more vulnerable: according to the French physician Chalin de Vivario, many succumbed to the plague because of the fears and imaginings produced by hearing funeral bells and morbid gossip. However, healthy living could offer some protection against infection, so that people were encouraged to keep their spirits up – much as we were encouraged to do during COVID-19 lockdowns. According to the Bolognese professor Tommaso del Garbo (c1305-70), the best ways to create joy and pleasure ‘during this time of pestilence’ included spending time with happy and carefree people, relaxing in the garden, and enjoying music and stories.

Keeping positive in the face of mass mortality was beneficial to all, but in non-plague times emotional wellbeing was particularly important for certain groups. Pregnant women, for example, were warned that ‘anger, deep sadness, fear, and similar emotions’ could kill a foetus, as could a sudden shock, such as a clap of thunder. Consequently, women who’d had multiple miscarriages were sometimes treated for melancholy, with their doctors seemingly viewing their mental state as the cause of, as much as a consequence of, their fertility issues. One Paduan woman named Elizabeth was told that her repeated losses probably resulted from excessive anger or sorrow, which drew the spirits away from the womb and made it too cold; only if her mental state improved would she be able to carry a pregnancy to term. In order to avoid such trauma, mothers-to-be were urged to ‘live in friendship with God and be merry’.

‘The exercise of the mind increases its strength to such an extent that many people are cured of their ills through sheer delight’

Medieval people were also very aware of the mental challenges they might face in their final years, including memory loss. According to the 11th-century Andalusian poet Samuel ibn Naghrillah, a man who lived into his 90s would inevitably be ‘beset with confusion, not knowing his left from his right’, while the future Pope Innocent III (1160-1216) claimed that old men were ‘easily provoked and hard to calm down’, moody and argumentative – and prone to ‘[praise] the good old days and hate the present’. In the most severe cases, individuals might lose the ability to perform their usual functions: Edmund Lacey, bishop of Exeter in 1420-55, was obliged to delegate most of his episcopal responsibilities from the late 1440s, at which time the mayor of Exeter observed that the elderly prelate ‘had no more understanding of the substance of this matter than the image in the wall-hanging there’.

According to the medical writer Gabriele Zerbi, author of Gerontocomia (1489), there were good physiological reasons for such age-related difficulties. He explained that old people were often forgetful ‘because cold and dryness are dominant in them’, and as the spirits became thick and sluggish, they also became dull-witted, fanciful, and depressed. But fortunately, just like their younger peers, the elderly could benefit from a healthy dose of pleasure, which improved their mental health as well as reducing pain and sluggishness; music (the effect of which on the mind and spirits was comparable to that of medicines on the body) was particularly good for them. Moreover, Zerbi claimed: ‘The exercise of the mind increases its strength to such an extent that many people are cured of their ills through sheer delight,’ with conversation, storytelling and maths problems all helping to keep an ageing mind active. In addition, many elderly people continued to work – most out of necessity, but some because they felt it was good for them. The poet Francesco Petrarch (1304-74), for example, ignored his friends’ urging that he should work less: he insisted that his studies were such a pleasure to him that ‘When I begin to rest and grow slow, I shall soon cease even to live.’

More than six centuries after Petrarch’s death, the mental health issues that troubled him and his contemporaries are still very much with us, so that, every year, millions of lives are touched by (and hundreds of thousands lost to) mental illness. Besides the immense personal cost, this epidemic also poses major challenges for society, placing a growing burden on our overstretched health services and overburdened economies. Consequently, it is of the utmost importance that everyone affected is able to access the best possible care, but, for many people around the world, the costs of doing so are prohibitive. Others have doubts about the wisdom of our current approach, highlighting the downsides of widely prescribed psychiatric drugs (which often have unpleasant side-effects, and which may work chiefly due to the placebo effect) and arguing that the overuse of diagnostic labels can sometimes do more harm than good.

So what, if anything, can we learn from medieval approaches to mental health that might improve the situation? Admittedly, there are many treatments – including exorcising demons, overdosing on saffron, and eating ostrich liver – that we should probably not revive. But we would, I think, do well to emulate our ancestors’ emphasis on preventive medicine, by focusing, both as individuals and as societies, on the connections and activities that build our mental resilience. There would also be obvious benefits to be gained from approaching mental health in a holistic manner, viewing it as a vital part of a healthy lifestyle rather than a standalone problem. But perhaps the most important lesson we can take from the experiences of Francesco Datini, King Duarte and the many other medieval people who struggled with their mental health is to remember that issues such as anxiety and depression are not a modern fad, but a perennial human problem.

Indigenous knowledge and art overwrite colonial cartography to correct the historical record in Central Australia

- by Aeon Video

Watch on Aeon
item.content:encoded:
‘The land had its own stories.’

A common narrative among European settlers was that the lands they occupied were empty and, therefore, free to claim. This assumption, imposed across many colonies, severed Indigenous peoples from places to which they held deep cultural and spiritual ties. Central Australia was no exception: the doctrine of ‘terra nullius’, used to justify British claims over Australia, treated the land as if it belonged to no one, disregarding the long histories of Aboriginal communities who had been living there for tens of thousands of years.

For this short documentary, the British artist Patrick Waterhouse collaborated with the Warlukurlangu art centre to revisit that history by intervening in official colonial documents and maps. Working for several years with Warlpiri artists from Yuendumu and Nyirripi, he invited them to respond to these archival materials through their own visual languages. The film captures the collaborative process, the conversations prompted by these documents and the striking works that emerge: pieces in which colonial cartography intersects with Indigenous knowledge and art.

item.title: Our eloquent hands
item.dc:creator: Alison Bashford
item.description:
Physicians reject palmistry as nonsense. But reading the creases of our palms for hidden meaning is what doctors have always done

- by Alison Bashford

Read on Aeon
item.content:encoded:
Listen to this essay

22 minute listen

Signs of the future are marked in our hands, or so any palmist will declare. But do hands also hold signs of the past? Do they have a history? Over decades of research as a historian of medicine and of human bodies, I’d never imagined such a niche question. And then it was sparked in an instant, between one second and the next, in the time it takes to open a manila folder. For another project altogether I was in the UK to research the papers of Charlotte Wolff, a physician trained in Berlin in the 1920s and living in London in the late 1930s, a Jewish refugee. Opening a file labelled ‘Zoo, 1938’, I came across a massive, delicate palm print: it belonged to Mok, a lowland gorilla at London Zoo. Two days after Mok’s death, the keeper had granted Wolff special permission to enter the morgue and collect a pattern that had been too dangerous to acquire in life.

Mok’s palm print was both forceful and touching. Indeed, I was tempted to literally touch, to hold hands across time, across species, and across the worlds of the living and the dead. The emotive power was unmistakeable, yet for all my training as a historian, it was inscrutable to me. I was also puzzled why Wolff, an exceptionally clever physician, seemed to be practising palm-reading, which today is associated with magic and the occult. Could there be such a thing as medical palmistry?

Over time, I learned that the answer is a clear, but unlikely, ‘yes’. Wolff was looking for the so-called ‘simian line’, a particular crease that some humans share with other primate species. Long ago, in embryonic time, the patterns on each of our tiny, clenched palms were formed. For most of us, three main lines were created. For some of us – up to 5 per cent – the so-called head and heart lines fused into a single crease stretching across the palm from one side to the other. Robert De Niro, Hillary Clinton and Benedict Cumberbatch each boast a simian line on their palms. Tony Blair apparently does on both hands, an even rarer distinction. In the 1920s, the London physician Francis Crookshank delighted in announcing that even the Virgin Mary had a simian line, directing people to see for themselves in Renaissance devotional art.

To this day, midwives still quickly check neonatal palms, not because the newborn might be divinely conceived, but because a single crease has a high incidence in those of us with a particular chromosomal anomaly known as trisomy 21. Not everyone with this transverse crease has Down’s syndrome. And not everyone with Down’s syndrome has the so-called (still-called) simian crease. And yet, so strong is the correlation that this sign on the hand was a key element of clinical diagnosis until recently. It is fair, if strange, to say that the history of palmistry is the history of medicine.

As a rule, physicians relish the weird in their own medical history, but I’ve learned that they don’t appreciate this particular claim. Yet, in turning their backs on the medical history of palmistry, they turn their backs on some towering figures.

In the summer of 1663 in Cambridge, young Isaac Newton walked over to the fair on Stourbridge Common and bought himself a new book, Palmistry, the Secrets Thereof Disclosed. It was written by a physician, who instructed that the lines, angles, shapes and hatches on the palm needed to be read strictly and precisely with a measuring compass. Here was a geometry of the hand that needed to be decoded mathematically. No wonder Newton was interested. Yet we also know that Newton attended to ‘occult’ knowledge that purported to be previously unknown or hidden, hence ‘secrets disclosed’. (In fact, physicians still use the word in that plain way: ‘occult pain’, for example, is of unknown or unseen origin.)

Newton was exercised by the learned traditions kept in ancient manuscripts and precious early printed books in Arabic, in Hebrew and in Latin, later circulating in vernaculars across Europe, the Middle East and North Africa. He was especially consumed by hermetic natural magic and the mysticism of ancient Jewish Kabbalah that had been Christianised in the Renaissance. This included what was then called ‘chiromancy’, discerning character, health and fortunes from the hand, from the Greek cheir. Medieval and early modern ‘prognostication’ – divining the future – was slowly turning into medical prognostics.

Most early chiromantic texts were written by physicians. From Paracelsus to the Paracelsian physician Robert Fludd, Newton had them all in his library. Sometimes the simian line was clearly illustrated, yet this particular sign had not yet been analysed by the comparative anatomists, the biostatisticians or the primatologists who would later name it.

Both folk palmistry and learned chiromancy were reference points for a modern anatomy of the hand

The hand has a history of natural magic and occult knowledges, but it is also just anatomy, and so it appears in a plainer anatomical canon too. Yet that tradition is enchanted in its own way. One of the 19th century’s most eminent anatomists, Charles Bell, wrote The Hand (1833), a medical text on God’s design. And not long after, humanity’s deep past was being re-told through the human hand. In The Descent of Man (1871), Charles Darwin recounted that, one day, standing upright, the hand of the primate called Homo sapiens was free to grasp and so to evolve differently, uniquely. It is no coincidence that it was in the 1860s that the term ‘haptic’ arose, from the Greek haptikós, not just to touch, but to grasp or perceive. The hand of this new species of primate was set free for matters beyond locomotion, ultimately giving humankind ‘universal dominion’ over all other creatures, as Darwin wrote, quoting Bell. What a revolutionary idea! Friedrich Engels certainly thought so, as he wrangled the human hand into his dialectics of nature, his search for the material drivers of history. Bell’s anatomical textbook had shown the human hand grasping that all-important tool.

Both folk palmistry and learned chiromancy were reference points for a modern anatomy of the hand. In the 1820s, the Czech anatomist Jan Evangelista Purkinje – known for his fingerprint studies – also analysed the crease patterns on human as well as monkey palms, specifying new terms: the lines of opposition, abduction, adduction, extension, and flexion. Yet, in order to clarify, he had to explain these as the life line, the line of Mars, the line of matrimony, the table line, the line of Venus, the line of Rascetta, and the lines of honour and fortune. Traditional palmistry, in other words, was his anatomical reference point. Nearly a century later, when a then-obscure English doctor named Reginald Langdon Down admitted a patient to the family’s private asylum, he recorded ‘Hands, no head line’ in the admission files. Palmists’ terms were his clinical referents too. That was in 1907, just after his own beloved son was born with the syndrome that was yet to be named for his family.

In France, the anatomist Paul Broca had for some time researched palm creases comparatively across humans and other primates, identifying ‘la disposition simienne du pli palmaire’. Over time, le seul pli – the single fold – was the term used in French scholarship, while German anatomists and clinicians referred to vierfingerfurche, the four-finger crease. In English and American studies ‘the simian line’ proved to be an enduring designation. In 1924, an anatomist employed by the London Zoological Society showed clearly that the orangutan had this single transverse line, and sometimes even two in parallel, both running right across the palm.

This was all on Wolff’s mind when she entered the morgue at London Zoo in 1938. Indeed, she had for some time been climbing into the primate cages taking the prints of every live simian she safely could: those of lemurs, spider monkeys, baboons, chimpanzees, orangutans and more. She even took the delicate prints of a hedgehog. Of more stature, perhaps, were the palms of human primates she collected and then interpreted. These were not any old Homo sapiens but very special specimens indeed. As I opened more manila folders in the Wellcome Collection, London, there were the intimate hand-portraits of every interwar cultural luminary imaginable: Aldous Huxley, Virginia Woolf, Vaslav Nijinsky, Maurice Ravel and so many more. Yet the most haunting remained Mok, the dead lowland gorilla.

It’s a delicate history to tell, this comparative anatomy across primate palms that gave rise to the offensive term ‘simian line’. Yet, before we object, sneer, mock, judge or even just enjoy this as the quirky business of early misguided medicine, or worse dismiss it as ‘pseudoscience’, we should note that this is not only an antique history. It tracks right up to our own present, involving some of the most distinguished researchers of the 20th century, Newton’s worthy intellectual descendants.

Around the same time that Wolff was taking Mok’s palm print, in another part of London the medical geneticist Lionel Penrose was beginning a lifetime assessing human palms and finger patterns. He was doing so both geometrically and statistically in a manner more sophisticated than, but not unlike, Francis Galton’s late-19th-century work on fingerprints. It is little known that Galton – often called the ‘father of fingerprinting’– took palm prints too, occasionally wondering if his hypothesis on the individuality of the fingerprint was also discernible in palm lines. This was a tradition of medical and genetic hand-reading that came to be called ‘dermatoglyphics’.

As late as 1990, the simian crease was even sought, detected and analysed prenatally, via ultrasound

In this context, it was the fortune of the so-called simian line to become the perfect exemplar of a classic modern biomedical pair, the visible ‘phenotype’ and its hidden twin, the ‘genotype’. The former is an observable physical trait; the latter is that trait’s unique DNA code or sequence. Sorting out the connection between them was a great driver of mid-20th-century genetics. Over the 1930s and ’40s, before the chromosomal cause of Down’s syndrome was known, clever Penrose could work only with the phenotype – the physical expression – and he was able to statistically correlate the simian line with the syndrome. And then, in the late 1950s, a Paris-based team discovered the genotype that was trisomy 21, the additional chromosome. It was a massive breakthrough, the long-invisible genotype (an extra chromosome) was now visible, a match with its long-visible phenotype (the simian line, le seul pli, vierfingerfurche). We might well say that an occult sign had been revealed.

I expected the medical palmistry – so to say – to then dissipate, to become antiquated, yet to my utter surprise it did not. For decades after the extraordinary chromosomal discovery, these world-leading Paris and London-based geneticists continued to exchange letters with diagrams of hand patterns, still drawing those three – and in some humans, just two – main lines on the palm.

In the 1960s, paediatricians added another palm crease of note, dubbing it the ‘Sydney line’, or sometimes ‘the simian-like line’. As late as 1990, the simian crease was even sought, detected and analysed prenatally, via ultrasound. One study showed that, in seven foetuses with this sign, four had no chromosomal anomaly, and three had trisomy 21. And even today, some of the most prestigious research hospitals in the world explain to parents that their neonatal physician may check the newborn palm, still nominating the ‘simian crease’.

We all know that a straight line can be drawn between any two points. But as a medical historian, can I really draw a line from Newton’s book Palmistry, the Secrets Thereof Disclosed to the prenatal detection of the simian line in the Journal of Ultrasound in Medicine? The first was built from knowledge that is far remote from our own comprehension of the human body. That was a world in which it made every sense that the planet Jupiter and the finger of Jupiter would be connected, a ‘sympathetic’ relation between a celestial macrocosm and a bodily microcosm. Yet I’ve come to appreciate that this apparently magical chiromancy is an archaic version of what modern clinicians do all the time and every day. They read bodily signs.

Medical students are routinely taught the distinction between a symptom felt by the patient, and a sign observed and interpreted by the clinician. This sign (a rash, the colour of nails, a black spot, a pattern in the palm) has that meaning (measles, liver disease, melanoma, Down’s syndrome). And so, all physicians are foundationally schooled in the interpretation of somatic signs. They are medical semioticians, whether or not they would put it that way.

All physicians are medical semioticians, professional and trained readers of bodily signs

The surprising thing is that some physicians put it precisely that way. It was initially strange to me that the London physician who observed the simian line on the Virgin Mary’s palm in the 1920s – Francis Crookshank – was also deeply schooled in the complexities of contemporary linguistics. Pondering the meaning of the simian line that some of his professional colleagues, as well as his patients, displayed, Crookshank began to insist that medicine desperately needed a ‘theory of signs’. One winter’s evening in 1926, he lectured on just that to the Royal College of Physicians and couldn’t understand why his medical brethren first rolled their eyes, and then closed their eyes, falling asleep with boredom. The connection he drew between clinical sign-reading and highly abstract semiotics was just too much. In so many ways, he was speaking a different language, and certainly his essay’s publication in the specialist book The Meaning of Meaning (1923) – to be read mainly by philosophers of language and Oxbridge cultural anthropologists – did nothing to persuade his medical colleagues. It may have been ill-delivered and badly pitched, but the fact is this palm-reading physician was theorising not just the simian line, but everyday clinical business: how signs on the human body are observed, named, and then ascribed meaning. He did so, not only, but not least for the simian line.

All physicians are medical semioticians, professional and trained readers of bodily signs. In his 16th-century treatise on chiromancy, Paracelsus claimed that ‘nothing is so secret in a human being that it does not have an outward sign’. Indeed, a whole language of the hand is discernible within the medical past. It was the 17th-century doctor John Bulwer who set out the origins of sign language in his enchanting book Chirologia, or the Naturall Language of the Hand (1644). He conceptualised the hand as a second mouth, so keen is its capacity to communicate by gesture and by sign. For Bulwer, it was the hand, not the mouth, that could speak a universal language, the ‘chiefest instrument of eloquence’. Two hundred years later, Bell, one of the greatest anatomists of his day, also wrote of the ‘eloquent’ hand. And a century after that, Wolff wrote about the psychoanalytic body that speaks, in A Psychology of Gesture (1945), placing her work on primate hands in just this tradition.

Today, some adventurous and imaginative medical schools take the connection between somatic signs, language and interpretation very seriously indeed, teaching physical examination through the idea of ‘The Body as Text’. ‘Every patient’s body tells a story,’ Stanford’s medical students are instructed. ‘The narrative includes the past and present of a person’s social and medical condition.’ Bulwer, Bell, Crookshank and Wolff would have added ‘and the future’: signs on the hand were not just diagnostic, but prognostic. The Stanford School of Medicine frames the physical examination as an old-school art that needs to be retained, not superseded, by various technologies that ‘see’ inside. This is the art, science and language of decoding the phenotype. It is quite right that Stanford explains this ‘body as text’ method as the interpretation of the phenotype. Yet when their clinicians teach this language of the body, they are perhaps unaware of just how long and distinguished the tradition of decoding somatic signs is.

When dead Mok’s hand first reached out to me – far more than a ghost – I was culturally cornered, stuck thinking that the palm was relevant only to palmistry. Yet of course the hand – including the fingerprints, the palm and its folds, creases and patterns – is plain human anatomy made semiotically and phenotypically meaningful. For centuries, fortune-telling palmists have studied the hand to unlock the future and the past, health and character, but so too have other experts in bodies and minds: physicians, psychologists, psychiatrists, embryologists, anatomists, endocrinologists, primatologists and physical anthropologists.

Having followed a language of the hand both backwards and forwards in time from Mok’s poignant print, it was especially affecting to learn that, as a medical elder in the 1970s, Penrose the curious geneticist was himself pursuing the history of palmistry: one of the final publications of his stellar career was on fingerprints and palmistry, published in The Lancet, no less. For me, Mok’s print became slowly unveiled from its occult state, no longer inscrutable and mysterious, but now known, legible, and clear, a historical secret disclosed.

After the photographs were released to the public, a Redditor combined several of them to create a dynamic image. In this video essay, the popular US YouTuber Hank Green makes the case that – like the famed ‘Earthrise’ photo, the ‘Pale Blue Dot’ image popularised by Carl Sagan, and the Hubble Deep Field pictures containing thousands of galaxies – watching this brief timelapse is an awe-inspiring experience, even if it doesn’t necessarily convey any new information. However, unlike those earlier images, its message isn’t one of our extraordinary smallness. Instead, with its dance of naturally occurring and human-made phenomena, the story it tells is one of our growing significance – for better and for worse.

item.title: Continental divide
item.dc:creator: Shawn Miller
item.description:
A century ago, the Pan-American road promised a new era of fraternity between the two continents. Did it succeed?

- by Shawn Miller

Read on Aeon
item.content:encoded:
Listen to this essay

26 minute listen

Leônidas Borges de Oliveira drove the first 300 miles of the world’s longest road trip alone. The date of his departure, in early 1928, meant that the young Brazilian army officer also had the road almost entirely to himself. This gave him time to think about what he had taken on. The vehicle beneath him, a donated Ford Model T with a decade of delivering newspapers on the odometer, chattered with ease over alternating segments of fresh gravel and steaming asphalt that constituted Brazil’s new highway, connecting Rio de Janeiro with São Paulo. On both sides of the road, Oliveira surveyed the deforested Paraíba Valley, which had hosted the world’s first coffee boom – ranks of bean-fruiting bushes whose product had reached global markets in 60-kilo sacks on the backs of mules. Oliveira was among the first to see his nation at highway speed, and velocity could make the eroded landscapes of the past feel irrelevant. He believed he was chasing the future.

His compatriots shared his optimism. With shining medals around his neck and a new Swiss chronograph on his wrist, Oliveira departed from Rio to the fanfare of two brass bands and a flourish of civic oratory. He arrived in São Paulo to cheering crowds and a press corps keen to follow his automotive exploits. Oliveira’s rapid progress on this first leg, not to mention his countrymen’s enthusiastic support, fortified his resolve to push on to his final destination: the United States’ capital at Washington, DC.

Oliveira’s inspiration to make the long drive sprang from a novel idea, first proposed in 1923: the construction of an automotive highway that would link up the Western Hemisphere with a long ribbon of asphalt. Nobody knew exactly where the proposal had originated, and some official reactions in Latin America were tepid, but the popular response revealed an accelerating enthusiasm, and auto makers moved to capitalise on it. In 1924, the US Department of Commerce, which was headed by former auto executives, welcomed delegates from 19 Latin American nations to the largest promotional junket the US had organised to date, including a greeting at the White House by President Calvin Coolidge and a month-long highway tour that circled from New York to North Carolina and Minnesota to Michigan. The objective was to promote what Americans were calling a ‘Highway of Friendship’ – a Pan-American road, from the northern reaches of Alaska to the tip of Tierra del Fuego, over which they hoped to see unfettered automotive travel and the emergence of stronger hemispheric cultural bonds.

Scores of intrepid adventure motorists were electrified by the possibility of such a road, and they believed the best way to support the proposal was to drive it, even before contractors had broken any ground. Oliveira, short in stature but ruggedly muscular, sought a little personal glory, he confessed, and none could blame him for that. But the notion that most resonated with his irrepressible idealism was the raw concept of unrestricted mobility, the agency and facility to go anywhere in the world a person cared to go. The last Western nation to abolish slavery, Brazil codified in its 1891 constitution every citizen’s right to move about the landscape without legal or physical restraint, and to reside, work and form relationships wherever they chose. For Oliveira, the highway and the car represented the medium and the means that could make free movement an achievable reality on a new scale. His long, goodwill drive was launched to celebrate these ideals, and to make them concrete.

What Oliveira ultimately wanted was an authentic Pan-American Union, two continents without passports, without customs, and without official barriers at the hemispheres’ many successive borders. Nearly a century later, the fraternal ideals that underpinned this dream and gave birth to the Pan-American Highway might appear unimaginably distant, subverted by nativist sentiment – but, in fact, remain alive in one of the two continents the road was supposed to link.

First, Oliveira had to prove it could be done. A few dozen had tried to reach the US before him. In fact, the first to road-test potential routes for such a highway were not American drivers in new American cars but Argentines and Brazilians piloting either luxury European sedans entirely inappropriate to the terrain or topless American jalopies of dubious reliability. Nobody had succeeded in – or even committed to, as Oliveira had – driving the entire expedition without a detour, that is, on the actual ground without placing one’s vehicle on the afterdeck of a ship or on a railroad flatcar to surpass a series of known, impenetrable topographies. Everyone told him, and kept telling him all along his route, that what he proposed was impossible. Brazilian highway officials doubted he would get out of Brazil.

He soon learned why he had so many doubters. Over his excursion, he found little mileage as easy as the Rio to São Paulo highway. The way was treacherous, and motorists had died in previous attempts. Indeed, Oliveira’s gruelling daily toil did not let up until he entered the US state highway system almost a decade later. His drive proved not only the world’s longest to date in accrued distance at 17,769 miles but also arguably the longest ever in elapsed time.

1 of 4

Oliveira’s convictions kept him and two later companions at their task, plodding north, year after year. At every opportunity, he spoke with energy about the dreams surrounding the construction of a highway connecting the continents, of an imminent hemispheric fraternity, and his remarks were published approvingly in papers in every nation he passed through. At his arrival in Washington, however, US officials insisted that what he claimed to have done was impossible. Most were considerate enough not to say it to his face, and he had the honour of meeting President Franklin Roosevelt and speaking to a large audience at the Pan-American Union building. But almost nobody believed Oliveira’s claims. Engineers from the US Bureau of Public Roads had struggled to walk segments of the route, let alone motor along it. And they rejected his maps, which they described as not inaccurate but belated. The Americans had already projected the official route through spaces their surveyors had not yet dared to go.

Where the road ran out, his men disassembled their vehicles, packed the components onto mules, and marched them on foot

The evidence, however, suggests that Oliveira did exactly what he said he did. He arrived in Washington in early 1938 with a 500-page logbook of his itinerary, as well as photographs of himself and his companions posing with every mayor, governor and head of state they met along their route. They took informal photos at train stations, each city’s name in prominent signage, to prove they’d been there. The streets of most towns and villages they passed through had never seen a car before, and Oliveira’s team was welcomed as conquering heroes. The Brazilians even had a formal portrait done in Managua with the Nicaraguan revolutionary Augusto Sandino, who was possibly the biggest obstacle to intercontinental automobile travel from 1927-33. Sandino had thwarted, captured and even shot previous automotive adventurers who’d dared to pass through his territory. The photo, taken while Sandino was in peace negotiations, was his last; he was assassinated two days later at a military camp, gunfire that Oliveira claimed to have heard himself.

In truth, Oliveira didn’t literally drive on four tyres over the entire route, though he cut no geographic corners. Where the road ran out or became too steep or narrow, his men disassembled their vehicles (he now had two Model Ts), packed the components onto mules, like sacks of coffee, and marched them on foot until the terrain again became drivable. As further proof, every step of the way, Oliveira’s maps detailed his progress, and he gifted copies of his charts to any state or national government that would receive them.

1 of 3

Beleaguered by a whisper campaign in Washington against his drive, Oliveira returned to Brazil disillusioned, and he rarely talked about his extraordinary excursion during the rest of his life, which was spent at the lowest rungs of Brazil’s consular service. Despite his inimitable effort, he had been disbelieved and called a charlatan. Even though he never seemed to raise the question himself, some at home wondered if his nationality, or worse, his likely African and Indigenous ancestry, played a role in his rejection as a legitimate explorer. And, despite substantial publicity, Oliveira’s expedition was largely forgotten, even in Brazil, not to be recovered in historical memory until this century.

The Pan-American Highway that Oliveira hoped to pioneer was indeed born in a burst of fraternal rhetoric. Officially, however, the road was never just about driving a car from Patagonia to Alaska, or vice versa, for the mere amusement of tourists. It was to be a modern network connecting every national capital, from Ottawa and Washington to Santiago and Buenos Aires. And this was to be only a beginning. The network was to then expand until it reached every province and shore, facilitating trade and resource extraction, breaking down old stereotypes and softening contested borders in friendly cultural exchanges. The ideals remained potent for half a century, and in 1966 the US declared the entire US interstate system part of the Pan-American Highway network.

In a strictly material sense, this greater project has been a remarkable success, millions of miles of functional automobile paths that have revolutionised movement and left few spaces inaccessible to wheels. By 1915, the US paved a road from Canada to Mexico. In 1917, Peru pushed its first highway into the Amazon Basin. Already by 1925, Venezuelans could drive over the Andes in comfort, and from 1931 Cubans could motor the full length of their island. The US built a primitive road across Canada to Alaska in 1942, during the war, and Mexican contractors reached Guatemala in 1950. The overall progress was extraordinary. Ironically, however, the key link in the system through Central America, over which the US took control and about which there was incomparable publicity, was the slowest to advance. Not till 1962 did the US-built highway reach Panama City. And not far beyond the Panama Canal, the road came to a sudden halt at the boundary of an almost mythical space between Panama and Colombia known from 1955 as the Darién Gap. Since about 1980, not a single mile of progress has been made to close it.

The Pan-American Highway would harden national borders almost everywhere it went, rather than open them

The idealised Pan-American Highway has a troubled history that in some essential features parallels Oliveira’s ill-starred excursion. The road was announced in celebration and extraordinary idealism; it was pursued despite extreme exertions, diplomatic squabbles and ballooning expenses; and its construction spanned an unexpectedly long period, essentially a century. But the project sputtered out in disappointment and forgetting. Remarkably, the highway ended in a broadly held false memory. If Brazilians forgot Oliveira’s record road trip, Americans seemed to remember that we finished the highway. Even today, two thirds of the North Americans I’ve asked if it’s possible to drive from North to South America think that the Pan-American Highway was inaugurated and has long been open to general traffic. This historical confabulation formed early. American tourists in the 1970s, some pulling camping trailers, drove south in full expectation of crossing the intercontinental divide to vacation in South America. When they passed through the Native village of Chepo in eastern Panama, locals kindly informed them that there was no road through, but third- and fourth-generation US motorists could not seem to comprehend the idea of no road, so on they went. One Chepo resident sardonically observed that, within days, every driver returned north by the same road they’d come on. Set straight about the highway’s incompleteness by their own experience, some expressed a sense of having been defrauded by all the official highway hoopla.

And just as Oliveira’s trip did not end in increased American brotherhood, the Pan-American Highway would harden national borders almost everywhere it went, rather than open them. If getting from one border to the next became increasingly easy, at the borders themselves, the road’s arrival threw up political, cultural and material barriers – walls, fences and even the Darién Gap itself, which at first was a geographical barrier universally condemned. By the late-1970s, the Gap came to be embraced as a permanent fixture by Panamanian officials, US diplomats and international environmentalists. The best current explanation for the highway’s unfinished status, the reason that Panama and Colombia are the only two bordering nations on Earth without an automotive connection of even the most rudimentary kind, is that Panama refuses to build a road they believe would serve as a superhighway for Colombian immigrants. The Gap is their border wall.

Before highways connected the nations of the Americas, many borders were illegible – nobody quite knew where the lines were, and states made little effort to monitor human ingressions into national territory. These official absences at the border reflected rather open policies toward immigration and naturalisation before the 1920s. Brazil’s constitution, like those of other Latin American nations, rejected colonialism’s restrictions on migration and guaranteed free entry to anyone ‘when and how he may choose, independently of passport.’ Many Latin American nations paid immigrants to come, and gave them free land on arrival. Even in border towns like the two Nogales – one in the Mexican state of Sonora, and the other in Arizona, US – people knew where the border was, but movement across it was brisk and unregulated. Residents shopped, courted, and attended school with little regard for the line, which ran down the middle of a broad, shared main street, and the cities’ two mayors shared fire-fighting resources and cooperated on policing crime. At Ellis Island, the first US federal processing centre for immigrants, and at other official entry points, millions arrived each year literally undocumented, without passports, visas or birth certificates. Their names, identities and even nationalities listed on ship manifests were whatever they cared to declare, and customs officers waved through nearly all of them with little ceremony beyond a hasty medical check.

Popular attitudes toward immigrants had fluctuated with economic conditions but, for decades, flaring anti-immigrant sentiment had had little effect on general policy. True, the US barred the entry of prostitutes in 1875, convicts and the insane in 1882, and polygamists in 1891, but other than the 1882 blanket ban on Chinese nationals, most legislation had rather narrow targets against individuals defined as undesirables. Otherwise, the doors were mostly open. Policies, however, changed abruptly in the 1920s, and the highway’s promotion had some impact on the reversal. The same year that Coolidge spoke in favour of building the highway, he also declared that ‘America must be kept American,’ and US Congress passed the broadly restrictive Johnson-Reed Act, whose discriminatory quotas reduced immigrant arrivals by a harsh 80 per cent. Latin Americans were not included in the act, but already by 1929 the US began detaining and repatriating individuals of Mexican descent, some of whom had been born in the US.

Changes in attitudes and policies were not restricted to the US: Mexico and Central America followed suit almost immediately. Panama barred West Indians from entry in 1926. In the early 1930s, Mexico not only halted Chinese immigration but expelled without due process thousands of Chinese residents, many of whom had established successful, multi-generational businesses. In some cases, border restrictions seemed to arrive simultaneously with the highway. Costa Rican officials, who had recently promoted their open borders, established their first, land-based immigration controls just as the US constructed the highway connecting the nation to Nicaragua and Panama in the late-1930s.

The barriers to migration were national, ethnic and racial, created to turn back the poor and car-less

Significantly, restrictions on entry did not apply to tourists. Nor to adventurers. At the time of Oliveira’s drive, one could still cross borders without being aware of them but, increasingly, legal admittance to a nation required both passports and visas, and the red tape could be thick. Still, Oliveira found no insurmountable official barriers to his expedition’s actual progress. Indeed, the best way to identify yourself as a safe holidaymaker, or a legitimate explorer – someone who posed little threat of overstaying one’s welcome – was to arrive at the border by car. The automobile signalled one’s status and, if passage by car was fast on the highway, entry was almost certain – if not quick and painless – once at the border.

But it was migrants, not tourists, who became the primary long-distance users of the Pan-American Highway and its tributaries. Despite motel construction and flashy campaigns promoting national scenic sites, automotive tourists never showed up in significant numbers on the road. This had less to do with the quality or unfinished status of the highway than with its extraordinary length. Boosters touted the highway as the world’s longest, expecting that moniker alone to draw motorists toward distant adventures, but the Pan-American Highway proved too long for the average American’s two-week paid vacation. Reporters imagined Ohio suburbanites driving to Rio de Janeiro as if on a whim. But a drive to South America, even without the inevitable hassle of shipping one’s car around the Darién Gap, was a commitment of many months, even if going just one way. The few who did get as far as Panama typically sold their cars to US military personnel in the Canal Zone and sailed or flew home because they could not face the hardship of driving all the way back.

So those who took to the road in their millions didn’t come in cars with sunglasses on their noses. Rather, they sought new homes far from the places of their chance births. The majority moved on foot from rural areas to the largest cities in their own nations, the great urban migration that began in the 1930s, explained in part by new industrial jobs but greatly facilitated by new roads. Others went greater distances to settle in neighbouring nations: Colombians to Panama City; Nicaraguans to San José; Paraguayans and Bolivians to Buenos Aires. The most adventurous made the long trip to the US. While the highway made movement overland for migrants on foot substantially easier, once they arrived at a border, they typically came up against formidable legal obstacles. Even if they had secured the proper papers, they might be rejected because, without cars, they were identified as poor migrants. The administrative barriers to migration were national, ethnic and racial in character but, most specifically, they were created to turn back the poor and car-less.

Hence, migrants circumvented officials by crossing borders where there were no roads. Nicaraguans arrived within view of Costa Rica on chartered buses that left them on a lonely highway that paralleled the border. Under the cover of night, they walked into Costa Rica where another bus picked them up and dropped them in San José the same day. Migrants moving north through Guatemala avoided the Mexican immigration office on the bridge over the Suchiate River, crossing the same on rubber rafts for a small fee, often within sight of authorities. To get across the US border, there were dozens of ways to get around official barriers, most of them now facilitated by Mexican cartels.

The longest walk still takes place in the Darién Gap between Colombia and Panama. Despite its distance and dangers, the Gap has been the most attractive point of entry onto migrant trails north because, without a road, neither Colombia nor Panama place officials or enforcement at the border itself, making it North America’s soft underbelly. Here, despite the hazards of the Gap, which includes a two-week trudge that has proven fatal for some, once at the border, you can walk across entirely unopposed. In the past, if Panama caught illegal migrants walking into the nation, they gathered them in jails and then marched them right back over the Gap. In recent years, with as many as a half a million coming through annually, including tens of thousands of children, Panama finds it easiest to put migrants on buses headed north, withholding passports until they arrive at the Costa Rican border.

Important elements of the highway’s original ideals have endured even in the face of the dominant, contrary trends in immigration policy. Strikingly, beginning in 2010, nations in South America that in the past had been at war, often over the very boundaries that separated them, states whose individuals still retain an often palpable dislike for one another, came together to agree that, for the purposes of immigration, their borders would essentially cease to exist. Agreements strove to recharacterise immigration as a solution rather than a problem: the free movement of people was likely to decrease national tensions, enhance labour allocation, and recognise migrants’ basic human dignity by eliminating discrimination in work, healthcare and civil rights. While the EU seemed to be suffering setbacks, such as the loss of the UK, South America quickly gained an almost universal adherence.

Hence today in South America, all those highways built at such great cost to connect national territories finally arrived at the destination to which Oliveira and others hoped: a union of American states. South America now houses the world’s largest free immigration zone, where the citizens of member nations, in addition to the familiar human rights of speech, religion, and assembly, now enjoy the basic right of free movement, to live, labour, and build (or reunite) families in any member country they choose. Regardless of their poverty, they can relocate to another nation without passports or visas and, upon arrival in their newly chosen home, they can start a business, send remittances, and enrol their children in public schools. Educational credentials are universally recognised, and new residents can be registered in national retirement programmes with credit for time employed in their nation of origin. And with just two years of residency, immigrants are eligible to apply for full citizenship. Nine nations have agreed to most of these terms, the exceptions being Venezuela, due to political challenges, and Suriname and Guyana, who are not yet parties to the treaty. The changes, of course, have not gone uncontested, particularly by conservative leaders such as Javier Milei, who insists on Argentina’s sovereign power over immigration, has suggested an Argentine Brexit, and even threatened Argentines with a loss of citizenship at home if they leave. Still, even in Argentina, the basic terms of the agreement hold, despite Milei’s populist bluster. The contrast with the US’s rising walls and Panama’s persisting Gap could not be starker.

In 1932, the Darién Gap was wider than it is today, and it was the only place that Oliveira was forced to backtrack. He attempted to drive it even though the Colombian military had told him it was impossible. Broad swamps and malarial fevers forced the Brazilians to place their disassembled Fords on the deck of a boat for the first and only time. Oliveira, who might be in the running for the most optimistic person to have ever lived, opined that the Pan-American Highway would never be built overland though the Gap. The topography, he believed, was just too difficult. On that point, he was wrong. Humans have built roads through, over, and under terrain far more difficult than the Gap: Mexico’s Durango to Mazatlán Highway conquers the Sierra Madre with 63 tunnels and 115 bridges, one of them 400 metres high; the Faroese have tunnelled 600 feet below the Atlantic Ocean to connect their remote islands, one segment of which includes the world’s first subseafloor roundabout.

In Panama, politics more than topography stand in the way of completing the road. The reality Oliveira could not yet see was that the fraternal ideals of free exchange and movement that he’d actively championed would die north of the Gap, foiling the highway’s long-anticipated completion. The South, however, has come to embrace Oliveira’s unswerving idealism, which would have pleased him. The myriad roads built across the South American continent in the past century, all without US help, permit the free flow of not just money, goods, ideas and wildlife, for which walls are mostly meaningless, but of human bodies, outside of whom no real meaningful rights exist. In South America, constitutional guarantees to free movement extend beyond national borders. Hence, a driving motive of the Pan-American Highway has now gone half the way there, but from the opposite direction its conceivers intended.

item.title: Upend the trickle-down
item.dc:creator: Les Coleman
item.description:
Neoliberal policies have hollowed out democracies and spawned unchecked oligarchs. Grasping their structure points to a fix

- by Les Coleman

Read on Aeon
