Listen to this essay

21 minute listen

If the people around you are spiteful and callous and will not hear you, fall down before them and beg their forgiveness; for in truth you are to blame for their not wanting to hear you.
– from The Brothers Karamazov (1880) by Fyodor Dostoevsky

If Western democracies were companies, they would be dismissed as lifestyle businesses whose managers (ie, political leaders) run them to promote their own interests and wealth. Leaders pursue projects that benefit the few, rather than national goals, and leave their countries with low economic growth, heavy debt and rampant white-collar crime. We entered this era of an unjust social order, political malaise and destabilisation almost half a century ago when the US president Ronald Reagan and the UK prime minister Margaret Thatcher introduced libertarian reforms that were embraced globally.

At his first cabinet meeting as president in 1981, Reagan distributed copies of Mandate for Leadership, whose 3,000 pages came out of the Heritage Foundation, a conservative research group in Washington, DC. This became the ideology of neoliberalism, which advocated a smaller state, industry deregulation, tax cuts, strengthened defence, and roll-back of social engineering. A year later, 60 per cent of the Mandate’s proposals had been adopted by the Reagan administration, and The New York Times called it ‘the manifesto of the Reagan revolution’. His initiative engaged Thatcher, and spread globally to dominate public policy in democracies around the world.

My perspective is that of an engineer with a career as a corporate strategist and, more recently, finance academic. In 2000, shortly after the Y2K scare, I left the corporate world for academia and research into decision-making by international finance organisations. In a round of industrial tourism, I interviewed more than 50 finance executives in Istanbul, London, Melbourne and New York. This led to three books, including Applied Investment Theory (2016), which criticised the justice system’s failure to prosecute corruption and criminal activity in large companies and among elected officials.

A framework used in corporate finance to explain the behaviour of organisations and individuals is the structure-conduct-performance (SCP) model, and it can help us understand the effects of the changes that Reagan and Thatcher brought to Western democracies. SCP conceptualises decisions within a multidimensional framework; when applied to countries, this framework postulates that their conditions are driven by the structure of institutions, laws and conventions; which drives the conduct or decisions of government, individuals and organisations; and that in turn leads to performance or outcomes.

Reagan and Thatcher asserted that unleashing markets and shrinking the state would ensure prosperity. Their signature initiatives of industry deregulation, tax reduction, market liberalisation and labour market reform won the day.

It did not take long, however, for the trickle-down effects of tax cuts funded by government debt to prove disastrous. Most obvious was the Black Monday stock market crash of October 1987. Neoliberalism had reduced the capacity of public institutions to manage systemic risks, and – as the authority and ability of government to regulate industry shrank – moral hazard spiked.

Infrastructure is a simple way to illustrate the realignment between state, markets and democratic institutions over the past half-century. Following the Second World War, Western governments invested heavily in transportation networks, energy systems and other public capital. Privatisation and deregulation reversed this trend, with cutbacks to public works projects: when roads and bridges, water systems and so on aged, productivity faltered.

Promises of prosperity by Reagan, Thatcher and other advocates of neoliberalism were mistaken because it brought only fragility to previously prosperous democracies. From an SCP perspective, the trickle-down of market liberalisation and financialisation brought slowing growth, rising debt burdens, institutional weakness, and declining public trust.

Some basic facts help to understand these claims, and give a sense of the impacts of neoliberal policies. Consider financial data since 1980 for the rich liberal democracies among the members of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD). Reduced tax revenue forced governments to rely on borrowings, and government debt – as shown in the left-hand graph of Figure 1 below – surged from 40 to 65 per cent as a share of GDP. Meanwhile, government expenditure kept pace with the economy at almost half of GDP.

In the right-hand chart of Figure 1 below, we see the economic consequences of high, unfunded government debt. The blue line tracks growth of GDP per capita, which gradually slowed from nearly 3 per cent annually in the 1980s to barely 1 per cent today. At the same time, deregulated credit markets encouraged households to borrow, and their debt more than doubled as a proportion of GDP. Quite obviously, neoliberalism did not deliver on its promises of economic growth and increased personal wealth.

The big winner from 50 years of neoliberal policy has been the finance sector. As government and household debt surged out of control, global capital became ever freer, bankers’ propensity for risk surged, and speculative activity flourished. Financial institutions grew dramatically in size and influence. In the US and the UK, financial institutions have become a power in terms of profits and political influence. But, as shown in Figure 2 below, they set up a roughly seven-year cycle of market bubbles followed by crash and recession, which created super, unearned wealth for investor elites. Meanwhile, the middle class and below saw home ownership and comfortable retirement drift out of reach, especially for Gen Y.

Probably the most powerful impact of neoliberalism has been on governance. Weakened corporate governance led to spectacular bankruptcies, with equally poor government strategy such as the failure to find promised weapons of mass destruction in Iraq, the 2008-09 global financial crisis, and over-the-top COVID-19 lockdowns. These generated anger and frustration that still linger, as indicated in Figure 3 above, where the rising global uncertainty index gives a rough but illuminating perspective on popular political sentiments.

The decline in the economic stability and health of Western political democracies over the past 40 years is not simply a run of bad luck, because it did not occur in countries such as China and India that resisted its blandishments. Bad decisions that inflicted sweeping damage to democracies came from deliberate structural misalignments between democratic institutions and social and economic realities.

Rectifying the malaise in Western political democracies requires realignment of the political paradigm, starting with support for decision-makers who can foster improved institutions and practices.

Though it may seem counterintuitive, we must raise the pay of top government officials. Consider the annual base salaries for heads of government of OECD member countries: around half fall in the range US$150,000-400,000; only Switzerland and Australia are higher, and the rest are even lower. The base salary of the US president has been fixed at $400,000 since 2001, while the UK prime minister’s salary of around £170,000 (cUS$230,000) is less today than that paid to Gordon Brown in 2009.

While money is not the only driver of occupational choice, underpayment invites mediocrity and the entitled, and encourages corruption. Political salaries need to be competitive. Leaders of government should be remunerated by reference to the compensation of CEOs of major domestic companies, with the pay of other politicians and senior government officials brought into line. In a mid-ranking country like Australia, trebling the base salary of members of the national parliament from a piddling US$170,000 per year would cost less than $80 million. That’s a cheap price for sound management of a $2 trillion economy.

Better-paid and better-financed candidates will help shake up the political duopoly

Voters paying their politicians more will expect better candidates and deeper competition. Their choices will be enhanced by more complete disclosure of candidates’ assets and interests, as required for candidates in India. Media denigration of politicians’ personal lives is an obvious deterrent to meritorious candidates. Australia has faced this, and allows individuals to sue for serious invasions of privacy when information relating to them has been misused.

The cost of election campaigns is another major impediment, especially to candidates from outside the establishment. Emerging candidates and parties would be helped by democracy vouchers as introduced in Seattle city elections, which are distributed to voters during election campaigns for them to support preferred parties or candidates.

Many democracies run longstanding two-party political systems: Liberal and Labor in Australia, Labour and Conservative in the UK, Republican and Democrat in the US. Even though parties swap government after every election or two, they co-ordinate through continual exchange of ideas. This duopoly structure stymies new directions and substantive reform (Noam Chomsky’s observation that ‘the smart way to keep people passive and obedient is to strictly limit the spectrum of acceptable opinion, but allow very lively debate within that spectrum’ comes to mind). Better-paid and better-financed candidates will help shake up the political duopoly and more closely review democracies’ performance.

Many politicians have a growth-first agenda. The Florida governor Ron DeSantis, for example, told his electorate: ‘We need a new generation of leaders who will promote policies that will foster economic growth.’ This imperative is important in light of the management truism that ‘what gets measured gets managed’, even when it’s pointless.

The most common measure of democracies’ performance is gross domestic product (GDP), which is a dumb yardstick because it simply records the value of goods and services that have a price. We get no information about their social or political meaning; nor details of other activities. As a result, unhealthy citizens, expenditure on wars, and rebuilding after accidents and disasters can all increase GDP. It does not count any value from the productivity and other benefits of free services such as the internet and AI (beyond their development and any subscription costs); nor does it count natural resources, unpaid labour or improvements in quality.

GDP growth at all costs encourages poor policy. Business corporations with a ‘triple bottom line’ such as profit, people and the planet better recognise social ideals than GDP. One country that acknowledges this is New Zealand whose Living Standards Framework measures the wellbeing of individuals and institutions as well as the country’s wealth. Such balanced measures should be a minimum standard for all governments.

Voters increasingly resent the burgeoning global oligarchy of the most wealthy and best-connected. Thus a survey across OECD countries in 2023 found that seven in 10 respondents want a more equal distribution of economic resources, and half think that disparities in political power are too high.

This concentration of wealth encourages oligarchs to protect their interests at the general community’s expense

Hard data back up these concerns. As shown in the left-hand graph of Figure 4 below, in large democracies, the share of total wealth held by the richest 1 per cent fell to its lowest levels around the mid-1980s. But it has rebounded since then: that 1 per cent now holds more than a quarter of total wealth in France, Germany and the US, and more than 20 per cent of the wealth in Australia, Italy and the UK.

This concentration of wealth encourages oligarchs to protect their interests at the general community’s expense. Most obviously, they introduced big money into politics, as evidenced by a US study in 2025, which found that 30-45 per cent of private contributions to presidential candidates come from the wealthiest 1 per cent of voters. Oligarchs have frozen out citizens and structured ‘cartel parties’ that use state resources for themselves.

Government economic policy is now a major source of oligarchs’ income. According to the management consultants McKinsey, higher government debt and easier credit increase financial assets in the private sector and promote asset price inflation. This disproportionately rewards wealthier households because they derive more of their income from financial, rather than labour, earnings. Similar benefit comes from corporate welfare, free markets and deregulation.

The benefit of increased government debt to wealthy households is confirmed in the right-hand chart of Figure 4 above. Since 1980, government debt in Western democracies almost doubled its share of GDP, while the proportion of wealth held by the top 1 per cent jumped by a quarter.

The risk from oligarchs’ power was summed up neatly by the futurist Aldo Grech: ‘Politics has been shaped through money and access’ and ‘a very small minority has steadily rewritten the rules that govern economics, labour, housing, healthcare, media, and even attention itself.’ The solution is to more closely tie wealth to its producer to limit its lifetime and stymie entrenchment of a hereditary ruling class. This would come from throttling excessive inter-generational transfers through a progressive death tax.

Many countries share the US experience that nothing seems to deter corporate fraud, systemic gambles and political misconduct. Congressional inquiries were all that confronted Enron and WorldCom, Wall Street and the financial crisis, Volkswagen’s emissions-test manipulation, big tech antitrust bills, and the opioid crisis. The US senator Elizabeth Warren expressed widespread frustration at ineffective control of such white-collar crimes when she pointed to blatant fraud during the financial crisis of 2008 and complained that ‘not one major bank executive was even charged, much less prosecuted and taken to trial.’ Two impediments are obvious.

First is the reigning medieval legal principle of mens rea (Latin for ‘guilty mind’) which makes conviction for crime contingent on proof of intent so as to distinguish criminal acts from accident or negligence. Intent is obvious with crimes against person and property, but it’s very difficult to prove with white-collar crimes such as fraud and market manipulations.

Strict liability should be extended to cover the fraud tolerated in many industries

A second impediment to prosecution of white-collar crime is the artificial separation between responsibility for regulatory breaches and criminal offences. As examples, workplace fatalities are investigated in most countries within a department of labour or similar; and financial fraud and misreporting are investigated by securities regulators. But regulators lack investigative expertise, can become too close to their industry, and can lack independence, as evidenced by the revolving door between them and the corporations they are supposed to be regulating.

The principle of mens rea and the bureaucratic investigation of white-collar crime protect well-connected criminals. Securing accountability requires the introduction of strict liability where individuals and relevant company officers become legally responsible for criminal and regulatory breaches. This already applies to most traffic, product liability and environmental offences, and last year the UK introduced a new strict liability corporate criminal offence of failure to prevent fraud. Strict liability should be extended to cover the fraud tolerated in many industries, and penalise criminal incompetence as evidenced by bankruptcy, workplace fatalities and the sale of faulty products. Defence would be confined to a reasonable belief that the action was legal, and intent is relevant only when determining the sentence.

Regulatory breaches and white-collar criminal offences should both be investigated by a common police force, independent of the crime and perpetrators. The best example is Singapore, whose police force has a Commercial Affairs Department that investigates a wide range of financial and corporate offences, including fraud, market misconduct and company law breaches.

Let us close with the oft-neglected ‘how’ of political transformation. In 1962, Thomas Kuhn wrote the book on its preconditions. The most relevant is accepting that the existing paradigm is ineffective, which is clear from voter dissatisfaction and loss of faith in leaders of the major democracies. As evidence, in elections held in 2024, voters around the world swung against the incumbent government in every developed country that held elections.

The times also favour structural political reform. In their review of the many elections of 2024, the Stockholm-based International Institute for Democracy identified ‘a profound and growing … sense that we are at a historical juncture where we must revisit and reassess the strength of our democratic culture and institutions.’ Moreover, today’s conditions resemble those of the dynamic Roaring 1920s, which also began after a shock pandemic, saw rapid introduction of new consumer technologies (cars, the telephone, movies, airplanes), cultural dynamism (jazz, Art Deco, Surrealism, psychoanalysis), as well as strong growth in economies and financial markets. The decade ended in the crash of 1929 and the Great Depression, but they were followed by sweeping political reform (Keynesian fiscal policy, adult suffrage, consolidation of political parties, and voter-driven initiatives).

There is no shortage of ideas to reform our democracies. Because voters acting as democratic troops in peaceful demonstration of mass dissatisfaction will always command attention, street protests involving at least 3.5 per cent of the population are almost guaranteed success. Other successful tactics include confrontational protests such as boycotts of elections, petitions and lobbying.

Tackling the crisis in democracy requires more democracy

Citizens’ assemblies are a promising path to political reform. These are best known in Ireland where 99 members of the public are randomly chosen to represent the country’s demography. They work like a super-jury to consider an issue over some days of meetings, and prepare a report with recommendations. Topics have included abortion, climate change, the challenges and opportunities of an ageing population, and drugs use.

Even these modest proposals threaten entrenched politicians and their parties, oligarchs and corporations. Opponents are so powerful and organised that reforming the democratic system inevitably requires securing insider support.

By the 20th century, Western democracies defeated the brutalities of material scarcity and political oppression. Today’s citizens are orders of magnitude better off than their ancestors in terms of income, technologies, health, and knowledge. Even so, aspects of basic wellbeing – such as rising income and affordable, quality housing – are receding for many. Performance has also been poor on non-economic measures such as public health, environmental quality, trust in science, and infrastructure reliability.

So, what happened? Recalling our structure-conduct-performance model, the short answer is that neoliberal reforms beginning in the 1980s weakened the institutions on which democracy depends. Tackling the crisis in democracy requires more democracy that breaks the monopoly position of ineffective incumbents and conservative duopolies. This comes through incentivising better-quality election candidates and alternative parties, modernising institutions, and rebalancing economic power.

item.description:
Hans Christian Andersen’s tantrum in Charles Dickens’s garden was a case of ‘too muchness’, emotions bursting past respectability

- by Siobhan Unwin & Kathryne Ford

Read on Aeon

Listen to this essay

22 minute listen

The English countryside in the mid-19th century could be an idyllic retreat. It is breakfast time and you are Charles Dickens, respectable author and exemplar of etiquette, sure that today will be safe and uneventful. Searching the house for your daughters, you also find your overstayed houseguest from Denmark, Hans Christian Andersen – famed author of fairy tales like The Little Mermaid and The Ugly Duckling – face down on the grass, in the middle of a complete meltdown on your lawn, after receiving news of a bad book review. The Victorian era remains the measuring stick for (ostensibly) respectable domesticity, where emotions are repressed and ankles sequestered in attempts at control. Nonetheless, here lies Andersen, actively proving that even great authors were one lawn tantrum away from tearing at this veneer of respectability.

And indeed, Andersen has since been headcanoned, with great enthusiasm, as a 19th-century ‘disaster bi’. A disaster bisexual is less an identity or a diagnosis than a way of reading scenes that spill over. Messy. Earnest. Intensely sincere to the point of social detonation. Seen in modern drama from Bridgerton to Saltburn, they are characterised by living, loving and feeling in a perpetual crescendo, then come to a full stop when they melt down.

The term circulates now as affectionate shorthand, especially online, for people and characters who come in too hot, overshare, and punctuate the resulting social chaos with wit. To the chronically online, Andersen’s correspondence, travels and attachments now read as exasperating yet endearing. But Dickens, that poor man, did not have Tumblr. What he had was a lawn.

As Dickens in 1857, you offer Andersen reassurance. Gentle reason. Perspective. After all, you understand the impact of a bad book review (the criticism of your 1844 novel Martin Chuzzlewit still stings). Nonetheless, your words barely clear the air before Andersen begins to weep. Not quietly. Not briefly. Not in a way that can be absorbed and moved past. A full-throated sob and a heavy stream of tears, earth streaked on his face and shirt. He stays there. The scene does not resolve. The emotional alarm bell keeps ringing, time stretches. Dickens’s daughter Katey stares, struggling to reconcile this sobbing spectacle with her assessment of their Danish guest as ‘a bony bore’. Dickens, the great manager of feeling in fiction, realises, with dawning horror, that he – despite priding himself on being the ‘Inimitable’ – has lost control of the atmosphere entirely.

We have all encountered an Andersen. Some of us have loved one. Some of us have been asked whether we really have the capacity to care for them. Some of us are an Andersen. We could treat Andersen’s collapse as a personality problem: a man who simply felt too much and too openly. But what makes the lawn tantrum intolerable is that the Victorian sense of propriety relied on tightly managed bodies, disciplined masculinity, and a strict division between private interior and public display. These expectations – the norms and scripts that still govern our modern social lives – buy into the fantasy that collapse can be avoided if only the most vulnerable behave better. The question is, when these scripts fail, whose collapse will we tolerate – and how many people will we lose by demanding composure?

The lawn, and situations like it, expose an impasse: what happens when feeling exceeds the social scripts meant to contain it. Neuroqueering – the practice of challenging norms about how bodies, minds and emotions should behave – makes that impasse visible, while neuroqueer excess offers a way to understand what spills beyond those norms.

Seeing Andersen and Dickens through the lens of neuroqueer excess is not an attempt to retrospectively diagnose or categorise them, but to use their scenes of overflow to consider how norms are enforced, resisted, and broken. Neuroqueering, as we use it here, is not an identity to be claimed so much as a verb, a doing.

On Dickens’s lawn, these rules are not theoretical. They show up as expectations: speak proportionately, recover quickly, be gentlemanly. Dickens thus acts not merely as a distressed host but as an enforcer of the Victorian norms that Andersen breaks.

This is where a neuroqueering approach changes the terms of the encounter. Instead of asking why Andersen cannot control himself, it asks why Dickens’s preferred forms of speech, feeling and recovery are treated as natural, proper and morally superior. Scholars such as Nick Walker and M Remi Yergeau examine how these often-invisible rules govern the ways bodies, minds and feelings are permitted to move through the world. Drawing on queer theory and neurodivergent ways of knowing, their work challenges the assumption that acceptable expression must be verbally fluent, emotionally proportionate, reciprocal, and delivered at the correct volume and moment.

Expressed by those on the margins, neuroqueer excess is a demand to be noticed and understood on their own terms

It is from this challenge that we propose the concept of neuroqueer excess. By excess, we do not mean flamboyance alone, nor pathology, nor a failure of self-regulation. Instead, neuroqueer excess is a kind of ‘too muchness’ that emerges when feeling, desire or embodiment refuses to stay within the narrow emotional constraints that society dictates. Unlike camp or queer transgression, neuroqueer excess does not rely on shared codes, irony or legibility; it often fails to be readable at all.

Expressed by those on the margins, it’s a demand to be noticed and understood on their own terms. Those who exist outside established norms of behaviour, dress and mannerisms become hypervisible and surveilled; an example could be effeminate men. Norms like these (for instance, heteronormativity and neuronormativity) can be subverted into an act of disruption and rebellion. Neuroqueer excess provides a way to read these scenes not as personal failures, but as moments where the limits of the social system are exposed.

Andersen’s humiliating and excessive public behaviour subverted 1850s English expectations of masculine restraint, composure and intimacy. Across a very different historical moment, the Australian performance artist Leigh Bowery is a useful parallel. His bold club attire and antics, carried out during the AIDS epidemic in 1980s Britain, troubled a later but no less exacting demand: that queer bodies remain discreet, manageable and quietly grateful for survival. Given that Bowery’s performances included explorations of bodily fluids, simulated birth, outrageous fashions drawn from the grotesque and the aspirational, pushback and containment by institutions was firm and final.

His nightclub, Taboo, was closed after The Mail on Sunday in June 1986 reported widespread drug use there. Later, Bowery’s performance at the Freedom Bar in Soho was reported as pornographic and cancelled by Westminster Council in November 1994. He died of AIDS-related illness five weeks later. It was Bowery’s aesthetic hyperbole – his distorted silhouettes, unapologetic flesh, theatrical filth and refusal of good taste – that proved intolerable because he refused to make himself palatable to those watching.

Seeing Dickens recoil from Andersen, and Britain recoil from Bowery, helps clarify what is at stake in neuroqueer excess across time. Each moment reveals a culture frightened by emotion that refuses to be shepherded back into scripts of propriety, productivity or resilience. Disaster bisexuality simply provides a contemporary name for that old terror: the subject who renders the atmosphere unmanageable. Victorian propriety, AIDS‑era respectability politics, and our present appetite for therapeutic neatness share a common demand: that excess be invisible or else useful. Tracing neuroqueer excess across these moments offers a diagnostic tool, revealing how norms become instruments of oppression, and which bodies and feelings they seek to discipline – on the lawn, in the university, or inside the nightclub.

Dickens was not simply enforcing these norms; he had built his life around them, which explains his discomfort at Andersen’s tantrum on his lawn. Charles John Huffam Dickens was a complicated character, who obsessively sought to control his legacy. Feelings of inferiority had haunted him since childhood, when his father was imprisoned for debt, and ever after Dickens (understandably) worried about money. Over time, as his celebrity as a writer increased, he learned how to control more narratives than those in his novels, selectively editing his life history to provide the illusion of a well-bred gentleman.

In 19th-century England, being a gentleman required more than money; it demanded strict adherence to often-contradictory codes of conduct, wherein family pedigree was also scrutinised. You wouldn’t find Dickens at his exclusive Athenaeum club in London discussing his paternal grandparents’ work in the service industry. No, they were conveniently elided.

Dickens was himself a man of intense emotions, who burned his draft autobiography because he couldn’t bear to recount the trauma of being rejected by his first love. (This painful part of his life was likewise excised. After all, it didn’t align with notions of 19th-century masculinity, which mandated emotional restraint and physical discipline – the so-called English ‘stiff upper lip’.)

Although the public might be secretly pining for scandal, they simultaneously demanded concealment

For an insecure gentleman committed to control, and accustomed to editing out inconvenient truths, Dickens was utterly unprepared for the egregious excess of Andersen’s lawn tantrum – his fellow author’s visceral response to a negative review in the papers. Andersen’s upper lip was quivering and covered in tears – openly exhibiting an ungentlemanly emotional outburst. Dickens’s instinctive response was to contain, quell and return order to his domestic domain. Even his subsequent advice to Andersen (likely intended to reassure) was delivered as a command to repress: ‘Never allow yourself to be upset by the papers …’ Refuse to feel.

Nonetheless, this experience with Andersen foreshadowed the public outrage coming for Dickens the very next year. Given his need for narrative authority, Dickens decided to set the record straight (or, as it turned out, decidedly crooked) when rumours of affairs were swirling amidst his marital breakdown. In June 1858, Dickens published a ‘personal statement’ in The Times, reminding his readers that such rumours were completely false and out of character for him. Unfortunately, the public reacted poorly – the scholar Robert Sawyer suggests that people were perhaps more disturbed by Dickens turning his private issues into public spectacle than by the behaviour itself.

Ironically, Dickens did have a mistress, an actress almost the same age when they met – 18 – as his daughter Katey. He went to great lengths to conceal her because, even though many men had mistresses, it wasn’t something that gentlemen broadcast in polite society. The Victorian veneer of respectability required private matters to remain private. Although the public might be secretly pining for scandal, they simultaneously demanded concealment. This provided a comforting illusion of middle-class Victorian domesticity, where the household functioned as a regulatory machine, grounding respectable society. After all, any unravelling of the domestic sphere would surely send the entirety of England spiralling!

These Victorian anxieties and competing impulses resonate today. At a Coldplay concert in Massachusetts in July 2025, the stadium camera landed on a man with his arms around a woman. The pair were Andy Byron, then chief executive of the data company Astronomer, and Kristin Cabot, its chief people officer. As soon as they realised that their embrace was being projected onto the jumbotron, Byron ducked out of sight and Cabot turned her face away. Coldplay’s Chris Martin joked from the stage that they were either having an affair or were simply very shy. The clip raced across social media, where online detectives identified the pair, investigated their private lives and transformed a few seconds of visible panic into a global morality play about an alleged affair. Both executives subsequently resigned. Yet the fascination lay not simply in what may or may not have happened between them, but in the spectacle of a carefully managed public surface suddenly collapsing. Under today’s norms, public displays of distress threaten to expose the precarious choreography sustaining the fiction that everything is under control.

Back to Andersen’s tantrum on Dickens’s lawn. The problem with the Danish writer’s meltdown is not that he is overwhelmed, nor even that he weeps. It is where this happens. Emotional expression was to be reserved for private spaces, while more public areas required restraint. The lawn bridges these realms – belonging to the domestic sphere, yet publicly visible – carefully designed to be seen and therefore to reflect the moral and emotional discipline of the household within.

A breakdown in a bedroom might be unfortunate but containable. A breakdown on the lawn ruptures the boundary altogether. Perspectives shift uneasily – who is responsible for restoring order? Dickens, as master of the house? Behind the scenes, however, his own household was deteriorating; he would separate from his wife the very next year. We might read Andersen’s meltdown on the lawn as marking the moment when the private secrets of Charles and Catherine Dickens’s home began to seep into public view.

It is tempting to imagine ourselves as more evolved than the Victorians, or more compassionate than Britain at the height of the AIDS crisis. We use gentler language now. We (allegedly) advocate for boundaries rather than etiquette, regulation rather than repression, self‑care rather than self‑command. But these are largely changes in vocabulary, not structure. The underlying demand remains strikingly consistent: that feeling be calibrated, legible, productive and contained. Emotional expression is encouraged, but only when it is proportionate, self‑aware, and oriented toward resolution. Distress must be narrated, not enacted; processed, not performed. Meltdowns are acceptable only in retrospect, rendered tidy through insight and growth. Unresolved or unresolvable excess is still treated as a failure of character.

You almost certainly know someone like this. The one advised to lower their voice. To first calm down. To abstain from mannerisms that are ‘girly’, ‘unladylike’ or ‘weird’. The one whose access to care, work or belonging is conditioned upon composure or obedience. Maybe that person is you.

Excess is not inherently virtuous. It is disruptive, exhausting, sometimes damaging to self and others alike

These norms are to our detriment. Neuroqueer excess is costly and destabilising, but it is also informative. It marks the precise points where our scripts for care, communication and belonging break down.

It is fashionable to treat figures like Andersen or Bowery as delightful radicals, icons of sincerity, or brave affronts to decorum. We must resist this temptation. Excess is not inherently virtuous. It is disruptive, exhausting, sometimes damaging to self and others alike. Andersen, Bowery and Dickens are more complicated than we can do justice to here. None of them emerges from this analysis as a moral exemplar. What they are, instead, are stress tests.

They show us what happens when bodies, affects, desires or ways of communicating exceed what a system can manage. And, crucially, they show us which lives are abandoned when systems fail. Victorian containment scripts did not spare Dickens embarrassment; they contributed to his own scandal. AIDS‑era respectability politics did not merely police aesthetics; they helped determine which queer lives were cared for, treated and mourned, and which were allowed to die amid moralised silence. Bowery’s excess unfolded in a Britain structurally incapable of caring for queer bodies without first demanding obedience, gratitude and discretion.

Our contemporary regimes are no kinder for being therapeutic rather than moral. Today, even with therapeutic discourse, neurodivergent and queer people are still routinely failed by scripts that demand self‑regulation, emotional legibility, resilience narratives, and ‘appropriate’ expression before care will be extended. And those who cannot comply? Like Andersen on the lawn, they become problems to be managed, weirdos to be excluded, and people to rush by in public spaces. Dickens, too, belongs among the failed as a man straining against contradictory societal regimes that lacked healthy emotional outlets. With Andersen, Dickens upheld the norms of his day. Later, the same norms would lead him to a scandalous fall, his missteps converted into public morality tales rather than recognised as the familiar fractures of containment under pressure.

What unites these figures is not heroism, but exposure. They reveal that our systems do not fail accidentally. They fail predictably, repeatably, along familiar lines, for similar people.

Neuroqueer excess teaches us that care cannot rely on scripts of propriety, productivity or emotional neatness. Excess will not always be ethical, enlightening or kind – sometimes, it will be unbearable. But refusing to sit with discomfort, insisting instead on rapid containment, has repeatedly left neurodivergent and queer people without care when it mattered most.

Care, here, is not indulgence. Nor is it discipline. It is something more fragile and demanding: the willingness to remain present when emotions spill past what we know how to manage.

Historically, neurodivergence and queerness were written about by those espousing neither identity, thus displacing the invaluable perspectives of people with lived experience. Recent work of groundbreaking neurodivergent and queer scholars offers the opportunity to redress this gap, seeking to understand people on their own terms. Sometimes referred to as testimonial justice, this emerging realisation requires shifting who speaks, who is listened to, and how we respond when they do. Important work remains, including mourning lost opportunities to empathetically engage with the figures in this essay. Testimonial justice requires us to pause before we interpret, to believe before we correct, and to follow rather than reshape what is being communicated. It requires making space for neurodivergent and queer people to define their own terms, building vocabularies without presuming a deficit, and resisting the impulse to smooth over what feels excessive, contradictory or unfamiliar. Instead, we can respond to excess by sitting alongside the person, resisting the assumption that they are broken, and suppressing our impulse to ‘fix’.

As Dickens, you stifle the instinct for decorum, deciding instead to engage in Andersen’s emotional excess

In other words, we get down on the lawn with Andersen, extending grace without requiring palatability – accepting that we may need to choose comfort within discomfort. Sitting quietly with Andersen, co-regulating on the grass. Engaging with Bowery’s art even amid simulated birth and enema water. The work of care inevitably feels inefficient, unsettling and unresolved – but that does not diminish its importance.

Let us now imagine an alternative lawn.

The same 19th-century morning in the idyllic countryside, and Andersen again undone on the grass, sobbing without measure or end. As Dickens, you stifle the instinct for decorum, deciding instead to engage in Andersen’s emotional excess. Despite still feeling somewhat awkward, you manoeuvre onto the lawn, accidentally leaving a muddy smudge as you pat Andersen’s back. Your friend looks at you, tear-stained and messy, and your initial response is revulsion. Pushing that first feeling away, you instead murmur: ‘It is indeed a most unfortunate review.’

And he replies: ‘I was so proud of it,’ before dissolving into tears again. You are painfully aware of your daughter Katey staring aghast at the scene.

Nothing is resolved. It looks wrong. Yet you stay there together, uncomfortable, and you do not leave. You do not speak over him, or force him inside, or let that moment end your friendship. Grass flattens beneath you both. Mud marks your clothes. The moment remains messy.

Perhaps it’s OK if the lawn is ruined.

item.dc:creator: Justin Neuman
item.description:
We are most human when we play freely, imaginatively, pointlessly. Gamification risks atrophying that most precious capacity

- by Justin Neuman

Read on Aeon
item.content:encoded:
Listen to this essay

18 minute listen

Our kids were playing Settlers of Catan over the holidays. Or rather, they weren’t. They’d rearranged the strategy game’s hexagonal tiles into an archipelago of islands that no rulebook recognises, imagined ‘bridges’ built from wood, brick and stone, and invented a purpose for the game about network connectivity that had nothing to do with earning points. They were not playing Catan. They were playing in Catan, using its materials as components to make a world the designers never imagined.

My first instinct was to reach for the rulebook and teach them how the game actually works. My next was to figure out how I could win. It took me a while to realise what I really needed to do: build up the courage to ask if I could sit in and build with them. That was the moment something shifted – not for the kids, who were already there, but for me: a 48-year-old professor sitting on the carpet, making islands and building bridges without a point in sight.

You can play a game or you can play in a game. When you follow the official rules, pursue the stated objective, and measure yourself against opponents or a scoring system, that’s competition: playing a game. The Greeks had a word for this kind of play: agôn, from the god who personified conflict, struggle and contest. But when my kids disassembled the board and turned it into a world, they were doing something older and stranger. They were engaged in what the French sociologist Roger Caillois, in his taxonomy Man, Play and Games (1958), called paidia: free, spontaneous, unstructured play. The kind with no winner, no score, and no optimisation. The kind of play that has almost no place in adult life and, arguably, the kind we need the most, especially now, when even our leisure comes with leaderboards.

The entire architecture of digital life – with its algorithmic feeds, frictionless production and the ambient expectation that we should be consuming or optimising at all times – nudges us towards chasing outputs rather than generating meaning. We track our sleep and score our calm. Fitness apps turn the morning run into a contest; meditation apps gamify stillness with streak counters; language apps award achievement badges for what used to be called curiosity. Even journaling apps nudge users toward consistency scores. The gamification of leisure has turned into work everything that used to exist as its counterpoint. Leisure has become a third shift with its own metrics, its own guilt, and its own sense of falling behind.

The philosopher C Thi Nguyen calls this ‘value capture’: the process by which a game’s simplified, legible values start to colonise the real-world activity the game was supposed to serve. Their power arises from the fact that games don’t just create worlds, but new visions of the good, telling players what to care about by virtue of what the game rewards through scores. When you’re doing Duolingo to maintain your streak, or when your place on the running app’s leaderboard replaces the reason you started running, that’s value capture. The metric ate the meaning.

The Dutch historian and cultural critic Johan Huizinga saw this coming almost a century ago. In Homo Ludens (1938), he argued that play is not marginal to civilisation but, rather, generative of it. For Huizinga, law, philosophy, poetry and war all emerge from play’s ‘magic circle’: the bounded space where ordinary rules are suspended and something else becomes possible. Huizinga worried that the play element had been declining in Western civilisation since the end of the 18th century, eroded by industrialisation and professionalisation. What he feared has now been fulfilled. It’s not that we killed play; we captured it and harnessed it to a productivity framework. Then we packaged and sold it for passive consumption. The magic circle was instrumentalised into a dopamine hit.

What’s missing is neither ‘fun’ nor ‘competition’. We have plenty of those and, to be clear, I’m a huge fan of both. I grew up playing soccer and skiing. In my teens and 20s, I was a serious rock climber. Later I evolved into a competitive ultramarathon runner and now have 50-plus races under my belt, thousands of miles on trails in my legs, and two age-group national titles to my name. Agôn is what I do on weekends. But it’s not where I find meaning, build community, or figure out who I am.

A large part of the trouble is that we’ve eliminated the conditions in which free play arises. Watch the subway car on any morning commute. Every head is bowed to a screen. Not working, not thinking, just filling the time. Candy Crush in the checkout line. Instagram between floors in the elevator. Mere seconds of unstructured time trigger panic, and our fingers reach unconsciously for our phones. But boredom isn’t a problem; rather, it’s the condition in which the mind, left alone, begins to play by itself, to wander, associate, drift toward the transitional space where unexpected connections assemble unbidden. Every moment that we fill with a screen forecloses the free play of the mind. We don’t just need different games. We need more nothing.

Minecraft (owned by Microsoft) and Lego are corporately branded IP ecosystems framed as toys for children

Caillois saw the full spectrum of play: from agôn (competition) and alea (chance), to mimicry (role-playing) and ilinx (vertigo and disorientation). All four types sit on a continuum between paidia (complete improvisation) and ludus (structured rules). However, contemporary game culture tends to collapse this entire spectrum into one narrow band: competition plus structure. We have no category (not in the App Store and not in our cultural vocabulary) for paidia without agôn: our culture has no home for free, exploratory, contemplative play that refuses to compete.

Of course, paidia still erupts wherever people stop keeping score: kids on a playground invent rules then abandon them mid-sentence, Minecraft’s creative mode hosts millions of players building dreamworlds for the sake of building; Lego, at its best, is a pure paidia portal – recombinatory, autotelic, improvisational. But these exceptions clarify the problem: Minecraft (owned by Microsoft) and Lego are corporately branded IP ecosystems framed as toys for children. It’s not that free play has vanished, it just exists under constant threat of value capture. We do it in spite of our platforms, not because of them.

Moreover, the kinds of play that refuse to compete or optimise, or produce a measurable outcome, lack cultural prestige and social infrastructure. The British psychoanalyst and paediatrician Donald W Winnicott would have recognised this absence as a clinical emergency. In Playing and Reality (1971), Winnicott argued that play is not what children do on the way to becoming productive adults; it is a crucial part of how human beings maintain their worlds. Through play we become present to our own experience, capable of surprise, alive to the difference between going through the motions and actually being there.

Winnicott’s key concept is transitional space, though ‘space’ is misleading here because he has in mind not a location but a condition. Think of a conversation so engrossing that you forget you’re speaking and say something you didn’t know you thought until you heard it leave your mouth. You’re not entirely inside your own head (fantasy) and you’re not entirely performing for an audience (compliance). You are in between. That in-between zone – neither fully private nor fully public, neither pure inner life nor pure external task – is what Winnicott called transitional space. It’s where creativity, art and what he called ‘imaginative living’ originate.

His most radical claim still hits like an urgent diagnosis: ‘It is creative apperception more than anything else that makes the individual feel that life is worth living.’ He contrasts this with compliance, a relationship to external reality that ‘carries with it a sense of futility’. It is worth pausing to unpack this fully. Winnicott is arguing that what makes life meaningful is ultimately not achieving goals, having a family or even making art. It’s about how we see the world. ‘Apperception’ names a mode of encounter in which perception is not passive reception but active engagement. The difference is subtle but decisive: in ordinary perception, the world is simply there and the self adjusts to it; in creative apperception, we co-create the world, forging something between self and environment in the zone of play.

Compliance, by contrast, is life lived on someone else’s terms, following scripts, bowing before scores and metrics: moving through a world already defined in advance. Nothing new is risked, nothing genuinely one’s own is made. Most people, Winnicott believed, experience just enough creativity to recognise its absence, sensing that they are mostly ‘living uncreatively, as if caught up in the creativity of someone else, or of a machine.’

That last sentence, written in 1971, strikes me as the most prescient insight from 20th-century psychology for our time. Long before the personal computer, before the algorithm, and before we voluntarily installed surveillance engines in our pockets and called them phones, Winnicott worried about being caught up in the creativity of a machine. He also had a solution: play. For Winnicott, play is the condition of feeling real on a daily basis.

Friedrich Schiller, writing almost two centuries before Winnicott, made the same case from the other direction. In On the Aesthetic Education of Man (1795), he argued that human beings are torn between the pull of raw sensation and the push toward abstract order, and that only what he called the ‘play drive’ integrates both. It’s a bold claim. Schiller wrote that ‘man only plays when he is in the fullest sense of the word a human being, and he is only fully a human being when he plays.’ Winnicott tells you what play does psychologically: it makes life feel real. Schiller tells you what it does metaphysically: it makes you whole.

Simply put: adults need play as desperately as children do – a zone where inner life meets outer materiality and something unpredictable emerges. The Greeks, of course, had a term for this. Aristotle’s medieval fanboy Thomas Aquinas identified eutrapelia, the habit of knowing when and how to play well, as a genuine and discrete virtue. A person who never plays is as disordered as one who never works. I’m not talking about ‘work-life balance’, an exhausted metaphor that still treats play as recovery time for the next productive thing. To practise the virtue of eutrapelia means that a good life requires play. You don’t earn it. You practise it, daily.

The question, then, isn’t whether to play. It is where does the practice live, and how can we regain it in our daily lives, and valorise it in our culture.

For years, I’ve commuted on foot from Grand Central Station to 14th Street, 30 blocks, give or take. I told myself it was exercise, or that I was saving the subway fare, or that I liked the air. But the truth is I was thinking. Or rather, I was letting thinking happen. The lecture I couldn’t outline at my desk would assemble itself somewhere around 34th Street, the important points falling into sequence with my footfalls, the argument clarifying as if the motion itself were doing the editing. I wasn’t working on the lecture. I was walking in it, the way my kids were playing in Catan.

Walking increased the capacity to generate multiple solutions to open-ended problems by 60 per cent

The experience is ancient and well-documented. Friedrich Nietzsche reputedly walked six to eight hours every day, and insisted in his Twilight of the Idols (1889) that ‘Only thoughts that come by walking have any value.’ Aristotle’s Lyceum was called the peripatetic school for its walkways (peripatoi). Jean-Jacques Rousseau claimed that he could compose only while walking. Albert Einstein walked from his home at Princeton, New Jersey to the Institute for Advanced Study and back each day, and supposedly told colleagues that the walk was where the real thinking happened; the office was where he wrote it down.

Contemporary research confirms these intuitions, this idea that walking is a form of play for the mind as well as the feet. In 2014, Marily Oppezzo and Daniel Schwartz at Stanford University found that walking increased divergent thinking – the capacity to generate multiple solutions to open-ended problems – by roughly 60 per cent. Curiously, a treadmill facing a blank wall worked nearly as well as wandering Stanford’s campus, suggesting that it’s the exercise, not the scenery, producing the results. Metronomic motion allows the thinking to arrive.

Push the body further and something stranger happens. Caillois’s taxonomy includes a category almost nobody talks about: ilinx, the play of vertigo and disorientation. Spinning until you’re dizzy. Or running past the point where the split times stop mattering and the self loosens its grip. I know this territory from the inside. The first question at the start of a 100-mile race isn’t whether your legs are ready. It’s whether your mind is: wanting to win might get you to the start-line of your local 5K, but agôn won’t get you to the finish of an ultra-marathon. And it’s a love of trails that makes those miles magical. Nguyen would call this striving play. The goal exists to make the experience of striving possible, not the other way around. The finish line is just the means; the journey is the destination.

Our son does something similar in our basement, though his materials are metal, wood and stone rather than miles of trail. He crafts with scraps of found steel, fixes electric motors, carves wooden animals, shapes copper into jewellery and stone into rings. Nobody assigned this. No tutorial dictates the sequence. The material teaches the craft: copper tells you what it wants to become; stone suggests a shape and you listen or it breaks. At the workbench, inner vision meets the friction of the physical world and something neither planned nor accidental emerges.

Wherever adults build or stumble into transitional space, play is doing its work even if we’re not keeping score

My son doesn’t sell what he makes. He gives it away: the knife to a friend, the carved animal to a teacher. Play pursued for its own sake, with no metric and no market, overflows into generosity precisely because nothing was extracted. When something beautiful emerges from a process that asked for nothing, the most natural thing in the world is to give it away. What he makes enters the world not as commodity but as gift.

I see the same dynamic at my day job, though, again, the materials are different. I’m a professor of literary studies, and the best sessions in my seminars have nothing to do with instruction. They obey the logic of improv: ‘yes, and’. A student notices something strange in a passage (a word that doesn’t fit, a silence where speech should be) and someone else picks it up, turns it over, connects it to something from three weeks ago, and suddenly the room is thinking a thought nobody walked in with. The seminar, at its best, builds transitional space inside an institution that mostly rewards compliance. It opens up the zone between private thought and public evaluation, where a student says something she didn’t know she believed until she heard it leave her mouth.

The same dynamic lives in a jazz combo finding a groove nobody charted, a graphic designer noodling with shapes until one surprises her, a group of friends kicking a ball around with no teams and no score. It lives in my son’s basement workshop and on the trail at mile eight, and in the 30-block walk where the lecture writes itself. Wherever adults build or stumble into transitional space – where inner life meets outer material and something unpredictable emerges – play is doing its work even if we’re not keeping score.

Aristotle thought that contemplation (theoria) was the highest human activity because it was done purely for its own sake, absorbing the entire human person. For centuries, and across domains of religion, the academy and the law, that hierarchy held, ranking the contemplative life above the active life, thinking above doing. But maybe the question itself is misleading. The question ‘What is the highest human activity?’ is itself a competition, an agôn. Play doesn’t enter that contest. Play dissolves it. Play is autotelic and relational, solitary and shared, serious and free; it refuses the binary.

Schiller, Huizinga and Winnicott were not wrong; play does makes life worth living. The capacity for play – the willingness to stop optimising, to sit on the floor, to walk without a destination, to make something and give it away – embraces a virtue with an old name: eutrapelia. It is the habit of playing well. The ordinary magic of being real.

item.description:
The nation’s water is secure, but its food is another matter: lessons from the city-state in efficiency versus self-sufficiency

- by Peter A Coclanis
